Rook matroids and log-concavity of PP-Eulerian polynomials

Per Alexandersson Address: Department of Mathematics, Stockholm University, SE-106 91 Stockholm, Sweden Email address: per.w.alexandersson@gmail.com and Aryaman Jal Address: Department of Mathematics, KTH Royal Institute of Technology SE-100 44 Stockholm, Sweden Email address: aryaman@kth.se
Abstract.

We define and study rook matroids, the bases of which correspond to non-nesting rook placements on a skew Ferrers board. We show that rook matroids are closed under taking duals and direct sums, but not minors. Rook matroids are also transversal, positroids, and bear a subtle relationship to lattice path matroids that centers around not having the quaternary matroid Q6Q_{6} as a minor. The enumerative and distributional properties of non-nesting rook placements stand in contrast to that of usual rook placements: the non-nesting rook polynomial is not real-rooted in general, and is instead ultra-log-concave. We leverage this property together with a correspondence between rook placements and linear extensions of a poset to show that if PP is a naturally labeled width two poset, then the PP-Eulerian polynomial WPW_{P} is ultra-log-concave. This takes an important step towards resolving a log-concavity conjecture of Brenti (1989) and completes the story of the Neggers–Stanley conjecture for naturally labeled width two posets.

Key words and phrases:
Matroid, transversal matroid, rook placement, lattice path, log-concavity, real-rootedness, partially ordered set, Lorentzian polynomials, Neggers-Stanley conjecture

1. Introduction

The distributional properties — unimodality, log-concavity and real-rootedness — of combinatorially defined sequences have been the focus of extensive research in the last decade [Brä15, AHK18, BH20, ADH23, Huh12]. A landmark result in this field dates back to Heilmann and Lieb’s theorem on the real-rootedness of the matching polynomial of a graph [HL72]. Later, Nijenhuis [Nij76] proved that the rook polynomial of a board is real-rooted, which corresponds to a special case of the previous result when the graph is bipartite. This was one of the early results concerning distributional properties of sequences in rook theory, which is concerned with enumerative aspects of rook configurations on a board. Since then, rook theory has been studied in various other contexts including Garsia and Remmel’s qq-rook theory [GR86], combinatorial reciprocity [GH00, Cho96] and the cohomology of a special class of Schubert varieties [Din97, DMR07].

In this paper, we draw a connection between rook theory and matroid theory, by considering non-nesting rook placements on a skew-shaped board; the combinatorics of these restricted rook placements is underpinned by a matroidal structure that we dub the rook matroid. We probe distributional properties of the corresponding non-nesting rook polynomial and show that while it is not real-rooted in general — for subtle reasons that relate to the Neggers–Stanley conjecture — it is always ultra-log-concave, a fact that we deduce from the Stanley–Yan basis-counting inequality for matroids [Sta81, Yan23]. The matroidal properties are similarly rich: rook matroids are transversal and bear a subtle relationship to another well-studied class of matroids defined on skew shapes: lattice path matroids [BdMN03]. We show in particular, that a single skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu supports two (generally inequivalent) matroidal structures and give a precise criterion for when they are isomorphic to one another. Curiously enough, this involves the quaternary matroid on six elements Q6Q_{6}.

Similar to lattice path matroids, rook matroids are seen to be positroids. Discovered and studied by Blum in the guise of base-sortable matroids [Blu01], positroids were reintroduced by Postnikov in [Pos06] as matroids that parameterize a certain stratification of the totally non-negative Grassmannian. These strata are the so-called open positroid varieties and their rich geometric properties closely mirror those of the well-studied Richardson varieties; a comprehensive algebro-geometric study of these objects was undertaken in [KLS13]. The multifarious combinatorial parametrizations of positroids—in terms of Grassmann necklaces, bounded affine permutations, Le diagrams, planar bipartite graphs and more—have since been thoroughly studied [Oh11, KLS13, HLO23]. We prove that rook matroids are positroids via Oh’s theorem [Oh11], the Grassmann necklace approach.

We then consider a poset-theoretic perspective of non-nesting rook placements by relating bases of a rook matroid to linear extensions of a corresponding width two poset. This allows us to show that for naturally labeled posets PP of width two, the PP-Eulerian polynomial WPW_{P} is ultra-log-concave. The context of this result is the Neggers–Stanley conjecture [Neg78, Sta86], which asserts that WPW_{P} is real-rooted. This was disproved by Brändén in 2004 [Brä04b] and by Stembridge in 2007 [Ste07], the latter of whom provided a naturally labeled counter-example of width two. By deducing the strongest possible distributional property for WPW_{P}, our results thus complete the picture of the Poset conjecture in the width two case. We do so by refining a well-known bijection between linear extensions of a poset and lattice paths to show that a certain multivariate analog of WPW_{P} — first defined by Brändén and Leander in [BL16]— is Lorentzian in the sense of [BH20].

The following is a summary of our main contributions together with the organization of the paper:

  • •

    In Section 2.1, we introduce our main combinatorial object – non-nesting rook placements on skew Ferrers shapes, its generating polynomial and compute a few examples. In Section 3.1, we define the rook matroid and study some of its structural properties: namely being transversal (Theorem 3.3), closed under taking duals and direct sums, but not closed under taking minors (Example 3.8).

  • •

    In Section 3.2, we characterize precisely when rook matroids are isomorphic to lattice path matroids, which is when the underlying skew shape does not contain 332/1332/1 as a subshape (Theorem 3.23). This criterion can be rephrased in terms of the rook matroid not having the matroid Q6Q_{6} as a minor. We also show that rook matroids generalize lattice path matroids in the following sense: lattice path matroids can be obtained as contractions of large enough rook matroids (Proposition 3.26). In Section 3.3, we show that the rook matroid is a positroid (Theorem 3.35). We then consider the Tutte polynomial of a rook matroid in Section 3.4 and show that it is the same as that of the corresponding lattice path matroid (Theorem 3.37).

  • •

    In Section 4 we prove that the non-nesting rook polynomial is ultra-log-concave via the Stanley–Yan basis-counting inequality (Corollary 4.2). We then consider the half-plane properties of lattice path matroids and give the first example of a lattice path matroid that does not have the half-plane property (Theorem 4.3). We also give new and self-contained proofs of the half-planeity of snake matroids and panhandle matroids (Proposition 4.8).

  • •

    In Section 5, we derive a bijective correspondence between skew shapes and width two posets that maps non-nesting rook placements to linear extensions, yielding a PP-Eulerian interpretation of the basis-generating polynomial of the rook matroid (Theorem 5.4). Consequently, the univariate polynomial WPW_{P} is ultra-log-concave which settles the log-concavity part of the Neggers–Stanley conjecture in the case of naturally labeled width two posets (Corollary 5.10); the log-concavity question has also been posed by Brenti [Bre89, Conjecture 1.1] and Brändén [Brä15, Question 2]. We also use this correspondence in the opposite direction to deduce enumerative information about the the non-nesting rook polynomial such as (a) an example of when it is not real-rooted (Corollary 5.13) and (b) a precise criterion as to when the non-nesting rook polynomial is gamma-positive (Corollary 5.16).

2. Preliminaries

In this section, we define the basic combinatorial objects that will be the focus of our interest: non-nesting rook placements on boards and their generating polynomials. We will also recall the necessary background on matroids and notions from the geometry of polynomials that will be used in later sections.

2.1. Boards, skew shapes and rook placements

We use [n][n] to mean the set {1,2,…,n}\{1,2,\dotsc,n\} and [m,n][m,n] to mean the discrete interval {m,m+1,…,n}\{m,m+1,\dotsc,n\}. The set of size kk subsets of [n][n] is denoted by ([n]k)\binom{[n]}{k}.

A board BB with rr rows and cc columns is a subset of the rectangular grid [r]×[c][r]\times[c]. We label the rows with elements from [r][r] and the columns with elements from [r+1,r+c][r+1,r+c] respectively, as in Example 2.1. The row labeling is done from the top to bottom and the column labeling is done from left to right. We refer to cells (i,j)(i,j) of BB with respect to this labeling until otherwise specified. For most of what follows, we restrict ourselves to special classes of boards coming from integer partitions.

An integer partition λ=(λ1,…,λn)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n}) is any non-increasing tuple of positive integers. Following the English convention, the Ferrers diagram of λ\lambda is a left-justified, weakly decreasing array of boxes. Two special partitions correspond to Ferrers diagrams in the shape of a staircase and rectangle, respectively. For the former, δn\delta_{n} denotes the partition (n,n−1,…,1)(n,n-1,\ldots,1) and for the latter, (a)b(a)^{b} denotes the partition consisting of bb parts each of size aa.

Given two integer partitions λ⊇μ\lambda\supseteq\mu of length at most rr, we let the skew Ferrers board associated with λ/μ\lambda/\mu be the board with cells

{(i,r+j):1≤i≤r​ and ​μi<r+j≤λi}.\left\{(i,r+j):1\leq i\leq r\text{ and }\mu_{i}<r+j\leq\lambda_{i}\right\}.

When μ\mu is the empty partition, we treat μ\mu as the all-zeroes vector. In what follows, we also refer to a skew Ferrers board as a skew shape. A subshape of a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu is the skew shape obtained by deleting rows or columns of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. The size of a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu is the number of boxes in its diagram and is denoted |λ/μ||\lambda/\mu|. An outer corner of λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a cell (i,j)∉λ/μ(i,j)\notin\lambda/\mu such that (i,j−1),(i−1,j)∈λ/μ(i,j-1),(i-1,j)\in\lambda/\mu. An inner corner of λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a cell (i,j)∉λ/μ(i,j)\notin\lambda/\mu such that (i+1,j),(i,j+1)∈λ/μ(i+1,j),(i,j+1)\in\lambda/\mu.

By a non-attacking placement of rooks on a board, we mean a configuration of rooks where no two rooks can take each other in the sense of chess. More formally, a non-attacking rook placement ρ\rho on a board BB is a subset of BB no two cells of which share a row or column index. Two rooks in a non-attacking rook placement form a nesting if one rook lies South-East of another. Hereafter, a non-nesting rook placement (or just rook placement, when it is clear that the setting is a non-nesting one) on a board BB is a non-attacking rook placement such that no pair of rooks forms a nesting.

We will frequently move between the settings of non-nesting rook placements and Dyck paths in a skew shape. A Dyck path in a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a lattice path starting from the Southwest corner of λ/μ\lambda/\mu and terminating at the Northeast corner of λ/μ\lambda/\mu that consists only of North and East steps. Examples can be found in Section 3.2.

We denote the set of non-nesting rook placements on a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu by NNλ/μ{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\text{NN}_{\lambda/\mu}} and define the generating polynomial of its kk-subsets as follows.

Definition 2.2.

Given a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu with cc columns, the non-nesting rook polynomial of λ/μ\lambda/\mu is defined by

Mλ/μ​(t)=∑k=0crk​(λ/μ)​tk,M_{\lambda/\mu}(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{c}r_{k}(\lambda/\mu)t^{k},

where rk​(λ/μ)r_{k}(\lambda/\mu) is the number of non-nesting rook placements on λ/μ\lambda/\mu of size kk. Note that the degree of Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} equals the length of the longest Northwest to Southeast diagonal that fits inside λ/μ\lambda/\mu, which is not necessarily equal to cc.

Example 2.3.

Let λa,b=(ab)\lambda_{a,b}=(a^{b}). Then we have

Mλa,b​(t)=∑k=0min⁡(a,b)(ak)​(bk)​tk.M_{\lambda_{a,b}}(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\min(a,b)}\binom{a}{k}\binom{b}{k}t^{k}.

This can be seen directly: choose a set {j1<…<jk}\{j_{1}<\ldots<j_{k}\} of columns in (ak)\binom{a}{k} ways and choosing a set of rows {i1>…>ik}\{i_{1}>\ldots>i_{k}\} independently in (bk)\binom{b}{k} ways. Form the rook placement with cells {(ik+1−ℓ,jℓ):ℓ=1,…k}\{(i_{k+1-\ell},j_{\ell}):\ell=1,\ldots k\}; by virtue of the ordering, this must be non-nesting.

By specialising a=b=na=b=n, we obtain the type B Narayana polynomial:

W⁡(t)=∑k=0n(nk)2​tk.W(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}^{2}t^{k}.
Example 2.4 (Narayana polynomials).

The non-nesting rook polynomial for the staircase Ferrers board λ=δn=(n,n−1,n−2,…,2,1)\lambda=\delta_{n}=(n,n-1,n-2,\dotsc,2,1) is

Mδn​(t)=t−1​Nn+1​(t),M_{\delta_{n}}(t)=t^{-1}N_{n+1}(t),

where Nn​(t)=∑k=1n1n​(nk)​(nk−1)​tkN_{n}(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{n}\binom{n}{k}\binom{n}{k-1}t^{k} denotes the nthn^{\textnormal{th}} Narayana polynomial. This can be seen by identifying rook placements on δn\delta_{n} with arc diagrams of a set partition and then using the standard bijection to show that non-nesting set partitions of [n][n] correspond to Dyck paths contained in δn\delta_{n}. (Recall that the Narayana polynomial NnN_{n} can be seen as the peak-generating polynomial of Dyck paths of size nn.) In this way, non-nesting rook placements on skew shapes generalize the study of non-nesting set partitions by considering general (skew) Ferrers boards in place of δn\delta_{n}. A leitmotif in this paper is a bijective correspondence between rook placements and lattice paths; a proof of this for general skew shapes can be found later in Proposition 3.11.

Distributional properties and multivariate generalizations of Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu}, together with its realizability as a PP-Eulerian polynomial of a poset, will be studied in later sections.

2.2. Matroids

We use the following axiomatization of matroids in terms of its bases; for any undefined terms hereafter we refer the reader to [Oxl11].

Definition 2.5.

A matroid MM is a pair (E,ℬ)(E,\mathcal{B}) where EE is a finite set and ℬ\mathcal{B} is a collection of subsets of EE, called bases, satisfying the following two properties:

  1. (1)

    ℬ≠∅\mathcal{B}\neq\emptyset.

  2. (2)

    For each distinct pair B1,B2B_{1},B_{2} in ℬ\mathcal{B} and element a∈B1∖B2a\in B_{1}\setminus B_{2}, there exists b∈B2∖B1b\in B_{2}\setminus B_{1} such that (B∖{a})∪{b}∈ℬ(B\setminus\{a\})\cup\{b\}\in\mathcal{B}.

The second property above is referred to as the basis-exchange axiom for matroids. Several other axiomatizations of matroids exist; an exhaustive list can be found in [Oxl11, Chapter 1]. One such axiomatization can be made in terms of independent sets. A set I⊂EI\subset E is an independent set of a matroid M=(E,ℬ)M=(E,\mathcal{B}) if I⊆BI\subseteq B, for some B∈ℬB\in\mathcal{B}.

An important example of matroids is the uniform matroid Uk,nU_{k,n}, defined as the matroid with ground set [n][n] and bases given by all kk-subsets of [n][n].

We briefly recount the various operations one can apply to a matroid to produce a new matroid.

  1. (1)

    Given a matroid M=(E,ℬ)M=(E,\mathcal{B}) and an element e∈Ee\in E, the deletion and contraction of MM by ee are the matroids with ground set E∖eE\setminus e that are respectively denoted by M∖eM\setminus e and M/eM/e and the bases of which are respectively given by:

    ℬ⁡(M∖e)\displaystyle\mathcal{B}(M\setminus e) ={B∈ℬ:e∉B},\displaystyle=\{B\in\mathcal{B}:e\notin B\},
    ℬ⁡(M/e)\displaystyle\mathcal{B}(M/e) ={B∖e:B∈ℬ,e∈B}.\displaystyle=\{B\setminus e:B\in\mathcal{B},e\in B\}.

    A matroid obtained from MM by a sequence of deletions and contractions is called a minor of MM. A class 𝒞\mathcal{C} of matroids is minor-closed if given a matroid M∈𝒞M\in\mathcal{C}, every minor of MM is also in 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

  2. (2)

    The dual of a matroid M=(E,ℬ)M=(E,\mathcal{B}) is the matroid M∗M^{*} on the ground set EE and bases ℬ⁡(M∗)={E∖B:B∈ℬ}\mathcal{B}(M^{*})=\{E\setminus B:B\in\mathcal{B}\}.

  3. (3)

    An element e∈Ee\in E is a loop of MM if ee appears in no basis of MM.

  4. (4)

    An element e∈Ee\in E is a coloop of MM if e∈Ee\in E appears in every basis of MM

  5. (5)

    The direct sum of matroids M1=(E1,ℬ1)M_{1}=(E_{1},\mathcal{B}_{1}) and M2=(E2,ℬ2)M_{2}=(E_{2},\mathcal{B}_{2}) is the matroid M1⊕M2M_{1}\oplus M_{2} with ground set E1⊔E2E_{1}\sqcup E_{2} and bases ℬ1⊔ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{1}\sqcup\mathcal{B}_{2}.

  6. (6)

    The single-element series extension of M=(E,ℬ)M=(E,\mathcal{B}), denoted S⁡(M,U1,2)S(M,U_{1,2}), is the matroid N=(E∪{f},ℬ′)N=(E\cup\{f\},\mathcal{B}^{\prime}), where

    ℬ′={B∪{g}:B∈ℬ,g∈{e,f}∖B},\mathcal{B}^{\prime}=\{B\cup\{g\}:B\in\mathcal{B},\,g\in\{e,f\}\setminus B\},

    and U1,2U_{1,2} is the rank 11 uniform matroid on ground set {e,f}\{e,f\} where e∈Ee\in E and f∉Ef\notin E.

  7. (7)

    Given a matroid M=(E,ℬ)M=(E,\mathcal{B}) of rank kk and an element e∉Ee\notin E, the free extension of MM by ee is the matroid M+eM+e on ground set E∪eE\cup e and bases

    ℬ(M+e)=ℬ∪{I∪{e}:|I|=k−1,I is independent in M}.\mathcal{B}(M+e)=\mathcal{B}\cup\{I\cup\{e\}:|I|=k-1,\,\text{$I$ is independent in $M$}\}.

Transversals of set systems give rise an important class of matroids. Given a set system 𝒩=(N1,…,Nr)\mathcal{N}=(N_{1},\ldots,N_{r}) of not necessarily distinct subsets NiN_{i} of some ground set EE, a transversal XX of 𝒩\mathcal{N} is a subset of EE consisting of rr distinct elements, one from each set in 𝒩\mathcal{N}: that is, X={ai:i=1,…,r}X=\{a_{i}:i=1,\ldots,r\} such that ai∈Nia_{i}\in N_{i} for i=1,…,ri=1,\ldots,r. A partial transversal of 𝒩\mathcal{N} is a transversal for some subsystem ℳ=(Ni)i∈J\mathcal{M}=(N_{i})_{i\in J} indexed by a subset J⊂[r]J\subset[r]. The following theorem due to Edmonds and Fulkerson laid the foundation for the theory of transversal matroids:

Theorem 2.6.

[EF65] The partial transversals of 𝒩\mathcal{N} are the independent sets of a matroid on EE.

Matroids that arise in this way are called transversal matroids and 𝒩=(N1,…,Nr)\mathcal{N}=(N_{1},\ldots,N_{r}) is called a presentation of the matroid. The bases of a transversal matroid are given by the maximal partial transversals of 𝒩\mathcal{N}. When 𝒩\mathcal{N} admits a transversal, the maximal partial transversals are precisely the transversals of 𝒩\mathcal{N}.

2.3. Real-rootedness, log-concavity and multivariate generalizations

In this subsection, we recall some basic notions in the geometry of polynomials.

Given a sequence of non-negative integers (ak)k=0n(a_{k})_{k=0}^{n}, it is convenient to work instead with its generating polynomial A⁡(t)=∑k=0nak​tkA(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_{k}t^{k}. The following notions, listed in descending order of strength, encode distributional properties of the sequence:

  1. (1)

    The generating polynomial A⁡(t)A(t) is real-rooted if AA has only real roots as univariate polynomial. Note that by the non-negativity of the aka_{k}, the roots of AA will necessarily be non-positive.

  2. (2)

    The sequence (ak)k=0n(a_{k})_{k=0}^{n} is ultra-log-concave if

    (ak(nk))2≥ak−1(nk−1)⋅ak+1(nk+1)for all 1≤k≤n−1.\left(\dfrac{a_{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}\right)^{2}\geq\dfrac{a_{k-1}}{\binom{n}{k-1}}\cdot\dfrac{a_{k+1}}{\binom{n}{k+1}}\quad\text{for all $1\leq k\leq n-1$.}
  3. (3)

    The sequence (ak)k=0n(a_{k})_{k=0}^{n} is log-concave if

    ak2≥ak−1⋅ak+1for all 1≤k≤n−1.a_{k}^{2}\geq a_{k-1}\cdot a_{k+1}\quad\text{for all $1\leq k\leq n-1$.}
  4. (4)

    The sequence (ak)k=0n(a_{k})_{k=0}^{n} is unimodal if there exists some 0≤m≤n0\leq m\leq n such that:

    a0≤a1≤…≤am−1≤am≥am+1≥…≥an.a_{0}\leq a_{1}\leq\ldots\leq a_{m-1}\leq a_{m}\geq a_{m+1}\geq\ldots\geq a_{n}.

The sequence (ak)k=0n(a_{k})_{k=0}^{n} has no internal zeros if

ai​aj>0⟹ak>0for all 0≤i<j<k≤n.a_{i}a_{j}>0\implies a_{k}>0\quad\text{for all $0\leq i<j<k\leq n$}.

As mentioned above, the following implications hold: (1)⟹(2)⟹(3)⟹(4)(1)\implies(2)\implies(3)\implies(4). Here (3)(3) implies (4)(4) only if (ak)k=0n(a_{k})_{k=0}^{n} has no internal zeros. For a comprehensive and modern survey of these notions, see [Brä15].

The sequence (ak)k=0n(a_{k})_{k=0}^{n} is palindromic if ak=an−ka_{k}=a_{n-k} for 0≤k≤n0\leq k\leq n. This is equivalent to the generating polynomial A⁡(t)A(t) satisfying tn⋅A⁡(1t)=A⁡(t)t^{n}\cdot A\left(\dfrac{1}{t}\right)=A(t). We will use the term palindromic for both the sequence and its generating polynomial. Any palindromic polynomial A⁡(t)A(t) can be expanded in the basis {ti​(1+t)n−2​i}i=0⌊n2⌋\{t^{i}(1+t)^{n-2i}\}_{i=0}^{\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor}:

A⁡(t)=∑k=0⌊n2⌋γk​tk​(1+t)n−2​k.A(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor}\gamma_{k}t^{k}(1+t)^{n-2k}.

If γi≥0\gamma_{i}\geq 0 for all i=0,…,⌊n2⌋i=0,\dotsc,\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor, then AA is said to be γ\gamma-positive. By pairing up reciprocal roots and noting that products of gamma-positive polynomials are gamma-positive, one can show that palindromic, real-rooted polynomials with non-negative coefficients are γ\gamma-positive.

Showing that a polynomial is real-rooted directly is often hard; multivariate techniques have streamlined and simplified these ideas.

Definition 2.7.

A polynomial P⁡(x1,…,xn)∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]P(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] is stable if

Im⁡(x1)>0,…,Im⁡(xn)>0⟹P⁡(x1,…,xn)≠0.\operatorname{Im}(x_{1})>0,\ldots,\operatorname{Im}(x_{n})>0\implies P(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\neq 0.

If all the coefficients of PP are real we say that PP is real stable. This will always be the case for us, and hereafter every instance of the word stable implicitly means real stable.

Real stability is a generalization of real-rootedness in the following precise sense: a univariate polyomial is stable if and only if it is real-rooted. Examples of stable polynomials include multivariate spanning tree polynomials, multivariate Eulerian polynomials and so-called Plücker polynomials: determinants of linear combinations of rank one positive semi-definite matrices [Brä15]. A less restrictive notion is that of Lorentzian polynomials.

Lorentzian polynomials are a class of multivariate polynomials containing stable, homogeneous polynomials and generalizing the notion of ultra-log-concavity. To define Lorentzian polynomials, we need two additional notions: that of MM-convex sets and the other of quadratic forms of Lorentzian signature.

Definition 2.8.

A finite set M⊂ℕdM\subset\mathbb{N}^{d} is MM-convex if for all α,β∈M\alpha,\beta\in M and i∈[d]i\in[d] such that αi>βi\alpha_{i}>\beta_{i} there exists j∈[d]j\in[d] such that αj<βj\alpha_{j}<\beta_{j} and α−ei+ej∈M\alpha-e_{i}+e_{j}\in M.

Definition 2.9.

A symmetric n×nn\times n matrix QQ with non-negative real entries has Lorentzian signature if it has exactly one positive eigenvalue.

By [BH20], the following can be taken as the definition of Lorentzian polynomials.

Definition 2.10.

A homogeneous polynomial P⁡(x1,…,xn)∈ℝ≥0​[x1,…,xn]P(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] of degree dd is Lorentzian if the following two conditions hold:

  1. (1)

    The support of PP is MM-convex.

  2. (2)

    For every α=(α1,…​αn)∈[d]n\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\ldots\alpha_{n})\in[d]^{n} with total sum d−2d-2, the quadratic form ∂αP\partial^{\alpha}P has Lorentzian signature. That is, the quadratic form ∂αP\partial^{\alpha}P has exactly one positive eignenvalue.

Important examples of Lorentzian polynomials include volume polynomials of convex bodies and projective varieties, and basis-generating polynomials of matroids [BH20].

3. The non-nesting rook matroid

In this section, we show that there is a natural matroid structure underpinning the set of non-nesting rooks on a skew Ferrers board. The associated class of matroids is a dual-closed subclass of both transversal matroids and positroids. However, it is not minor-closed and therein lies the subtlety in the relationship between rook matroids and lattice path matroids. The schematic in Figure 1 summarises the various containment and characterization properties that rook matroids satisfy with respect to other known classes of matroids; we will prove these in Sections 3.2 and 3.3.

We begin by studying the structural properties of the rook matroid that arise from its transversal description.

3.1. Structural results

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape. Throughout we draw and refer to Young diagrams λ\lambda and μ\mu in terms of the English convention, that is as a left-justified array of boxes. With this convention in place, we index the rows of λ/μ\lambda/\mu by {1,2,…,r}\{1,2,\dotsc,r\} and the columns by {r+1,…,r+c}\{r+1,\dotsc,r+c\}, and we set

Eλ/μ≔{1,2,…,r}∪{r+1,…,r+c}.{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}E_{\lambda/\mu}}\coloneqq\{1,2,\dotsc,r\}\cup\{r+1,\dotsc,r+c\}.

Given a non-nesting rook placement ρ\rho on λ/μ\lambda/\mu, we associate to it the set R⁡(ρ)∪C⁡(ρ)R(\rho)\cup C(\rho) where R⁡(ρ)R(\rho) is the set of row indices occupied by ρ\rho and C⁡(ρ)C(\rho) is the set of column indices that are not occupied by ρ.\rho. First note that for each non-nesting rook placement ρ\rho, we have that |R⁡(ρ)∪C⁡(ρ)|=c|R(\rho)\cup C(\rho)|=c, the number of columns of the shape. We gather these sets into a single collection :

ℛλ/μ≔{R⁡(ρ)∪C⁡(ρ):ρ∈NNλ/μ},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}}\coloneqq\{R(\rho)\cup C(\rho):\rho\in\text{NN}_{\lambda/\mu}\},

where as before NNλ/μ\text{NN}_{\lambda/\mu} is the set of non-nesting rook placements on λ/μ\lambda/\mu.

Secondly, we note that the correspondence ρ↦R⁡(ρ)∪C⁡(ρ)\rho\mapsto R(\rho)\cup C(\rho) is bijective.

Lemma 3.1.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape. The map from NNλ/μ\text{NN}_{\lambda/\mu} to ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} defined by ρ↦R⁡(ρ)∪C⁡(ρ)\rho\mapsto R(\rho)\cup C(\rho) is a bijection.

Proof.

Note that this map can be written as

(1) {(i1,j1),…,(ik,jk))}↦{i1,…,ik}∪([r+1,r+c]∖{j1,…,jk})\{(i_{1},j_{1}),\ldots,(i_{k},j_{k}))\}\mapsto\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{k}\}\cup([r+1,r+c]\setminus\{j_{1},\ldots,j_{k}\})

which is clearly injective. The inverse map takes the set of occupied rows and unoccupied columns {i1,…,ik}∪{jk+1,…​jc}\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{k}\}\cup\{j_{k+1},\ldots j_{c}\} to ρ={(i1,ℓ1),…,(ik,ℓk))}\rho=\{(i_{1},\ell_{1}),\ldots,(i_{k},\ell_{k}))\}, where {ℓ1>ℓ2…>ℓk}\{\ell_{1}>\ell_{2}\ldots>\ell_{k}\} is the set [r+1,r+c]∖{jk+1,…,jc}[r+1,r+c]\setminus\{j_{k+1},\ldots,j_{c}\}. The order on the column indices ℓs\ell_{s} implies that that ρ\rho is a non-nesting rook placement. ∎

In the light of Lemma 3.1, we can speak of ρ\rho and R⁡(ρ)∪C⁡(ρ)R(\rho)\cup C(\rho) interchangeably.

Given a skew shape, we may define a set system as follows. For j∈[c]j\in[c], let AjA_{j} be the set of row indices occupied by column r+jr+j together with r+jr+j, that is

Aj={i∈[r]:(i,r+j)∈λ/μ}∪{r+j}.A_{j}=\{i\in[r]:(i,r+j)\in\lambda/\mu\}\cup\{r+j\}.

Then 𝒜λ/μ≔(A1,…,Ac){\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{A}_{\lambda/\mu}}\coloneqq(A_{1},\dotsc,A_{c}) is a set system on Eλ/μE_{\lambda/\mu} which defines a transversal matroid, which we also denote by 𝒜λ/μ\mathcal{A}_{\lambda/\mu}.

Example 3.2.

Consider the skew shape λ/μ=77553/42\lambda/\mu=77553/42.

This skew shape has corresponding set system

Theorem 3.3.

The set ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} is the set of maximal partial transversals of the set system 𝒜λ/μ\mathcal{A}_{\lambda/\mu}. In particular, ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} is the set of bases of a transversal matroid on the ground set Eλ/μE_{\lambda/\mu}.

Proof.

Let 𝒯λ/μ\mathcal{T}_{\lambda/\mu} be the set of transversals of the set system 𝒜λ/μ.\mathcal{A}_{\lambda/\mu}. We claim that the map ρ↦R⁡(ρ)∪C⁡(ρ)\rho\mapsto R(\rho)\cup C(\rho) is the necessary bijection from NNλ/μ\text{NN}_{\lambda/\mu} to 𝒯λ/μ.\mathcal{T}_{\lambda/\mu}. Given a non-nesting rook placement ρ\rho, the set R⁡(ρ)∪C⁡(ρ)R(\rho)\cup C(\rho) is indeed a transversal of 𝒜λ/μ\mathcal{A}_{\lambda/\mu} since we choose i∈Aji\in A_{j} if there is a rook in column r+jr+j and row ii; if column r+jr+j is empty, we choose r+j∈Ajr+j\in A_{j}. Further, by Lemma 3.1 we know that this map is a bijection, so it suffices to show that every transversal of 𝒯λ/μ\mathcal{T}_{\lambda/\mu} is of the form R⁡(ρ)∪C⁡(ρ)R(\rho)\cup C(\rho) for some ρ∈NNλ/μ\rho\in\text{NN}_{\lambda/\mu}.

Suppose we are given a transversal TT of 𝒜λ/μ\mathcal{A}_{\lambda/\mu}. The fact that the row indices in TT correspond to distinct sets of 𝒜λ/μ\mathcal{A}_{\lambda/\mu} implies that TT defines a rook placement ρ\rho on λ/μ\lambda/\mu —possibly containing nestings—with no rooks in the column indices of TT. We need to show that ρ\rho can be transformed into a non-nesting rook placement. This will follow from the claim below.

Claim: Let the occupied row indices be ordered as r≥i1>i2>⋯>iℓ≥1r\geq i_{1}>i_{2}>\dotsb>i_{\ell}\geq 1. Then

(2) i1∈A1,i2∈A2,…​iℓ∈Aℓ.i_{1}\in A_{1},\;i_{2}\in A_{2},\;\dotsc\;i_{\ell}\in A_{\ell}.

Proof of claim: Suppose that we have ik∈Ami_{k}\in A_{m} and im∈Aki_{m}\in A_{k} for some k<mk<m. This corresponds to placing rooks on the squares marked in the diagram below, where we have used k′k^{\prime} and m′m^{\prime} for r+kr+k and r+mr+m respectively. By virtue of the cells (im,k′)(i_{m},k^{\prime}) and (ik,m′)(i_{k},m^{\prime}) being occupied and the board being a skew Ferrers board, we know that the cells (im,m′)(i_{m},m^{\prime}) and (ik,k′)(i_{k},k^{\prime}) must also lie on λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Thus by swapping the row indices of the two rooks we can be sure that the rook configuration is still contained within λ/μ\lambda/\mu with the same unoccupied columns and with one less nesting. That is, ik∈Aki_{k}\in A_{k} and im∈Ami_{m}\in A_{m} and this proves the claim.

By performing a sequence of such swaps for each pair of nested rooks, we can ensure that (2) holds, thus canonically realizing the transversal TT as a non-nesting rook placement ρ\rho on λ/μ\lambda/\mu. ∎

Identifying the resulting matroid by its set of bases, we call ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} the rook matroid on λ/μ\lambda/\mu; for any matroid MM, we say that MM is a rook matroid if it is isomorphic to a rook matroid of the form ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}. The uniform matroid Uk,nU_{k,n} corresponds to the rook matroid on the (n−k)×k(n-k)\times k rectangle. Later on, we will see how rook matroids interact with other well-studied classes of matroids, including lattice path matroids and positroids.

Remark 3.4.

It is natural to ask if the skew shape assumption is necessary in the above theorem. The answer is yes; consider the board BB in Figure 2 below.

If NN​(B)\text{NN}(B) denotes the set of non-nesting rook placements on BB, then the collection of would-be bases of the rook matroid on BB is (with same order as in Figure 2):

{R⁡(ρ)∪C⁡(ρ):ρ∈NN​(B)}={456,146,256,246,245,346,126,234}.\{R(\rho)\cup C(\rho):\rho\in\text{NN}(B)\}=\{456,146,256,246,245,346,126,234\}.

However, this does not satisfy the basis-exchange axiom: 6∈{1,4,6}∖{2,3,4}6\in\{1,4,6\}\setminus\{2,3,4\} but neither of {1,4,2}\{1,4,2\} or {1,4,3}\{1,4,3\} are contained in the collection above. Indeed, neither of 142142 nor 143143 can represent a valid non-nesting rook placement on BB. This fact—together with the argument in the proof above that allows us to interpret any transversal of 𝒜λ/μ\mathcal{A}_{\lambda/\mu} as a non-nesting rook placement by carrying out swaps— emphasizes the importance of the board being a skew shape in order to support the structure of a rook matroid.

More can be said about the transversal structure of the rook matroid. A fundamental transversal matroid is a matroid MM that has a basis BB (called a fundamental basis) such that each cyclic flat FF of MM is spanned by some subset of BB. An equivalent characterization identifies fundamental matroids as those transversal matroids that have a presentation (A1,…,Ac)(A_{1},\ldots,A_{c}) such that for each j∈[c]j\in[c] there exists an element i∈Aji\in A_{j} such that i∉Aki\notin A_{k} for all k∈[c]∖{j}k\in[c]\setminus\{j\}. This allows us to immediately note that rook matroids are fundamental transversal, as the distinguished element in each set of the presentation of ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} is simply the associated column label. The fundamental basis of the rook matroid then corresponds to the empty rook placement. See [BKdM11] for more about fundamental transversal matroids.

Lemma 3.5.

The class of rook matroids is closed under direct sums.

Proof.

A direct sum of rook matroids corresponds to the rook matroid on the direct sum of the corresponding skew shapes. That is, if λ1/μ1\lambda_{1}/\mu_{1} and λ2/μ2\lambda_{2}/\mu_{2} are two skew shapes, then the direct sum λ/μ≔(λ1/μ1)⊕(λ1/μ1)\lambda/\mu\coloneqq(\lambda_{1}/\mu_{1})\oplus(\lambda_{1}/\mu_{1}) is obtained by positioning the North-East corner of λ1/μ1\lambda_{1}/\mu_{1} to the immediate South-West of the South-West corner of λ2/μ2\lambda_{2}/\mu_{2}; see Figure 3. Then by the obvious isomorphism, ℛσ≅ℛλ1/μ1⊕ℛλ2/μ2\mathcal{R}_{\sigma}\cong\mathcal{R}_{\lambda_{1}/\mu_{1}}\oplus\mathcal{R}_{\lambda_{2}/\mu_{2}}. ∎

We now examine rook matroids through the structural properties of being dual-closed and being minor-closed. The former is rather straightforward while the latter turns out to be quite subtle.

The conjugate of a partition λ\lambda is the partition λ′\lambda^{\prime} obtained by taking the transpose of the Ferrers diagram of λ\lambda. Duals of rook matroids are simply rook matroids on conjugated shapes.

Proposition 3.6.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape and let λ′/μ′\lambda^{\prime}/\mu^{\prime} denote its conjugate. Then the following isomorphism holds: ℛλ/μ∗≅ℛλ′/μ′\mathcal{R}^{*}_{\lambda/\mu}\cong\mathcal{R}_{\lambda^{\prime}/\mu^{\prime}}.

Proof.

Suppose λ/μ\lambda/\mu has rr rows and cc columns. Define a map f:[r+c]→[r+c]f:[r+c]\to[r+c] by

f⁡(i)={i+c,for i∈[r],i−r,for i∈[r+1,r+c].f(i)=\begin{cases}i+c,\quad&\text{for $i\in[r]$},\\ i-r,\quad&\text{for $i\in[r+1,r+c]$.}\end{cases}

Then ff is clearly a bijection that sends rows and columns of λ/μ\lambda/\mu to columns and rows of λ′/μ′\lambda^{\prime}/\mu^{\prime} respectively. This corresponds to conjugating the skew shape and thus ff is the necessary isomorphism. See Figure 4 for an example. ∎

The following lemma shows that minors of rook matroids — in two cases — are straightforward to describe combinatorially. We make use of this lemma several times throughout the paper.

Lemma 3.7.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape and ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} be the corresponding rook matroid. Suppose xx is a row index and yy is a column index of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Then

  • •

    The deletion ℛλ/μ∖x\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}\setminus x is isomorphic to the rook matroid obtained from the shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu with row xx removed;

  • •

    The contraction ℛλ/μ/y\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}/y is isomorphic to the rook matroid obtained from the shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu with column yy removed;

  • •

    The bases in the contraction ℛλ/μ/x\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}/x correspond to non-nesting rook placements on λ/μ\lambda/\mu where row xx is occupied by a rook;

  • •

    The bases in the deletion ℛλ/μ∖y\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}\setminus y correspond to non-nesting rook placements on λ/μ\lambda/\mu where column yy is occupied by a rook.

Proof.

This follows directly from definitions. ∎

We turn our attention to the property of being minor-closed, which fails for rook matroids. This can be seen by taking any extension of the lattice path matroid 𝒫332/1\mathcal{P}_{332/1} that happened to also be a rook matroid; see Example 3.8. The deeper reason for this failure is best understood in terms of the observation that minors of fundamental transversal matroids are rarely fundamental transversal.

Example 3.8.

Consider λ/μ=3322/22\lambda/\mu=3322/22, the skew shape shown in Figure 5 and M=ℛλ/μM=\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}. The matroid M∖6M\setminus 6 can be seen to be isomorphic to 𝒫332/1\mathcal{P}_{332/1}, which is not a rook matroid. This is because the only possible candidate is ℛ332/1≅Q6\mathcal{R}_{332/1}\cong Q_{6} (proven below), which is a known excluded minor of lattice path matroids. Thus M∖6M\setminus 6 is not a rook matroid and rook matroids are not minor-closed11 1 We thank Joe Bonin for suggesting an example that did not rely on exhaustive computer search, and for pointing out that the class of rook matroids on 332/1332/1-avoiding skew shapes is not minor-closed. as was claimed in an earlier version of this manuscript..

Below, we show that matroid ℛ332/1\mathcal{R}_{332/1} is isomorphic to Q6Q_{6}, the quaternary matroid of rank 33 on 66 elements. To see that Q6Q_{6} is not a lattice path matroid, it suffices to note than Q6Q_{6} is an excluded minor for the class of lattice path matroids; see [Bon10, Theorem 3.1] where Q6Q_{6} appears in the list as A3A_{3}. For further properties of Q6Q_{6}, see [Oxl11, pg. 641].

Lemma 3.9.

The rook matroid ℛ332/1\mathcal{R}_{332/1} is isomorphic to the quaternary matroid Q6Q_{6}.

Proof.

By checking the three element circuits of each matroid, it is not hard to see that the map from {1,2,…,6}\{1,2,\ldots,6\} to {a,b,c,d,e,f}\{a,b,c,d,e,f\} defined as 1↦c,2↦f,3↦d,4↦a,5↦b,6↦e1\mapsto c,2\mapsto f,3\mapsto d,4\mapsto a,5\mapsto b,6\mapsto e is a matroid isomorphism between ℛ332/1\mathcal{R}_{332/1} and Q6Q_{6}. ∎

We will return to the link between 332/1332/1-avoiding shapes and lattice path matroids in Section 3.2 by considering the representation of a lattice path as a permutation.

3.2. Relation to lattice path matroids

In what follows we collect enumerative and matroidal results linking rook matroids to lattice path matroids, a well-studied family of transversal matroids that also arise from skew shapes. The goal of this subsection is to identify precisely when a rook matroid and a lattice path matroid on the same skew shape are isomorphic.

By lattice path we always mean a path from (0,0)(0,0) to some integral endpoint consisting only of North and East steps. We will identify a lattice path with its set of East steps; note that this convention differs from the traditional treatment of lattice path matroids in [BdMN03, BdM06], where North steps identified a lattice path. Since lattice path matroids are a dual-closed class of matroids, this point of difference has no structural consequences. We use the convention of East steps to make clear a certain bijection between rook placements and lattice paths that we define later.

Let m,r≥0m,r\geq 0 and U,LU,L be two lattice paths from (0,0)(0,0) to (m,r)(m,r) such that UU never goes below L.L. Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be the skew shape defined by the region enclosed by UU and LL. Lattice paths can be uniquely identified by the set of their east steps in the following way. For a given lattice path LL, traverse LL from the bottom left corner of λ/μ\lambda/\mu to the top right and record the indices of the East steps taken. See Figure 7 below for an example.

Denote by M⁡[U,L]M[U,L] the transversal matroid on [m+r][m+r] with presentation given by ℰ=(E1,…,Em)\mathcal{E}=(E_{1},\ldots,E_{m}) where EjE_{j} are East step sets defined by

Ej={i:i is the index of the jth East step of some lattice path P in λ/μ}.E_{j}=\{i:\text{$i$ is the index of the $j^{\textnormal{th}}$ East step of some lattice path $P$ in $\lambda/\mu$}\}.
Definition 3.10.

A lattice path matroid (LPM) is a matroid that is isomorphic to the matroid M⁡[U,L]M[U,L] for some lattice paths U,LU,L.

To emphasize the perspective of the matroid arising from a skew shape we will instead use the notation 𝒫λ/μ≔M⁡[U,L]{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu}}\coloneqq M[U,L], where U,LU,L are respectively the upper and lower boundary paths of the diagram defined by the skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu. With this choice we will be studying only loopless and coloopless lattice path matroids since UU and LL never share a step.

Note that when μ\mu is the empty partition, the lattice path matroid 𝒫λ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda} is called generalized Catalan matroid [BdM06] or Schubert matroid.

Our first result connecting rook matroids and lattice path matroids is a straightforward bijection, that naturally leads to the question of when they are isomorphic.

Proposition 3.11.

For any skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu, we have that the sets of bases of 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} and ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} have equal cardinality.

Proof.

Given a lattice path inside a skew shape, a cell of the skew shapeis a valley if it is immediately above an East-North segment of the path. It is straightforward to see that if we know the location of the valley squares, we can recover the path. Note also that valleys of a path must be located in a non-nesting configuration. Thus given a path, we simply place a rook in each of its valleys in order to produce a non-nesting rook placement. See Figure 8 for an example. Conversely, given a non-nesting rook placement, we fix the valleys of the path precisely at each cell containing a rook. The non-nesting nature of the rook placement ensures that this a valid lattice path. ∎

Remark 3.12.

In particular, when λ\lambda is the staircase (n,n−1,…,1)(n,n-1,\dotsc,1), we obtain the bijection described in Example 2.4.

For the exact count of the number of lattice paths contained in λ/μ\lambda/\mu, there is an elegant determinantal formula that can be deduced from the Lindström-Gessel-Viennot lemma, see [Kra15, Theorem 10.7.1] and [SP02, Eq. (6)] for example.

Observe that the bijection in Proposition 3.11 is not a matroid isomorphism in general, since the outer corners–to–rooks bijection described above was not shown have been induced by a bijection between the groundsets of the matroids. The goal for the remainder of this subsection is to characterize when ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} and 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} are isomorphic. As we noted in Section 3.1, the obstruction to this isomorphism comes from the skew shape 332/1332/1 where the lattice path matroid structure and rook matroid structure are not isomorphic. The more surprising fact is that this is the only obstruction for a rook matroid to be a lattice path matroid.

The next sequence of results develops the tools needed to define this matroid isomorphism, using the combinatorics of skew shapes. The first notion involves dividing up the skew shape into rectangles.

Definition 3.13.

The rectangular decomposition of a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu is the collection of rectangles partitioning the skew shape, each of which is formed by grouping together columns that share the same set of row indices.

An example of the rectangular decomposition of a skew shape is shown in Figure 11. We use the rectangular decomposition to give a characterization of 332/1332/1-avoiding skew shapes, that is the class of skew shapes not containing 332/1332/1 as a subshape. The following proposition gives two ways of describing this class.

Proposition 3.14.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a connected skew shape. Then the following are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    The shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu is 332/1332/1-avoiding.

  2. (ii)

    The shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu can be built from the skew shape consisting of a single cell by using a sequence of following four operations: (I) duplicating the first row, (II) duplicating the last column, (III) adding a box to the first row, (IV) creating a new first row with a single box. These four operations are illustrated on the shape below:

to8.17776pt{\hss\ignorespaces\hss}\vss}\kern-8.58658pt\vrule height=8.58658pt,width=0.40881pt\kern 8.17776pt\vrule height=8.58658pt,width=0.40881pt}\kern-0.2044pt\kern-8.58658pt\hrule width=8.99539pt,height=0.40881pt\kern 8.17776pt\hrule width=8.99539pt,height=0.40881pt}\cr}}\kern 1380.4pt}}$}\quad\text{respectively}.
  3. (iii)

    The rectangular decomposition of λ/μ\lambda/\mu satisfies the property that for any three consecutive rectangles R1,R2,R3R_{1},R_{2},R_{3}, we do not simultaneously have that

    1. (a)

      the top of R1R_{1} is strictly above the bottom of R3R_{3},

    2. (b)

      the top of R1R_{1} is strictly below the top of R2R_{2},

    3. (c)

      the bottom of R3R_{3} is strictly above the bottom of R2R_{2}.

Proof.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu occupy rr rows and cc columns. The equivalences are clear if either r≤2r\leq 2 or c≤2c\leq 2, so assume for the remainder of this proof that r,c≥3r,c\geq 3.

(i)⟹(i​i)(i)\implies(ii) Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape not satisfying (iii). We must show that the diagram must then contain 332/1332/1 as a subshape. We may assume that λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a minimal shape having this property. (Here by minimal with respect to its size |λ/μ||\lambda/\mu|) t

By minimality and the assumption above, this implies that λ/μ\lambda/\mu must satisfy the following properties:

  1. (1)

    The first two rows of λ/μ\lambda/\mu have different length.

  2. (2)

    The last two columns of λ/μ\lambda/\mu have different length.

  3. (3)

    The first and second row have their last cells in the same column.

  4. (4)

    The first row contains more than one box.

Property (1) and (3) imply that λ/μ\lambda/\mu has an inner corner at the first row; let the corresponding column index of that corner be kk. Let the common column index in which the first two rows have their last cell be jj. The last two columns of the skew shape will then be j−1j-1 and jj. By property (2), columns j−1j-1 and jj have different length which implies that λ/μ\lambda/\mu has an outer corner in column jj; let the corresponding row index of that corner be s≥3s\geq 3, by the assumption on the number of rows and columns. Then λ/μ\lambda/\mu contains 332/1332/1 as a subshape since it has an inner corner at (1,k)(1,k), an outer corner at (s,j)(s,j) and columns kk to j−1j-1 — which by the assumption r,c≥3r,c\geq 3 are at least two in number — all have the same length.

(i​i)⟹(i​i​i)(ii)\implies(iii) Proceed by induction on |λ/μ||\lambda/\mu|; the base case holds vacuously. Assume the result holds for all skew shapes with size less than |λ/μ||\lambda/\mu|. Let the skew shape λ1/μ1\lambda_{1}/\mu_{1} be the shape before λ/μ\lambda/\mu to which one of the operations (I)-(IV) was applied and let 𝒟\mathcal{D} and 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} respectively be the collection of rectangles in the rectangular decompositions of λ/μ\lambda/\mu and λ1/μ1\lambda_{1}/\mu_{1}. Consider the operation that transformed λ1/μ1\lambda_{1}/\mu_{1} to λ/μ\lambda/\mu. If it was (I), then duplicating the top row maintains the relative heights of any three rectangles in 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} and hence (iii) holds for 𝒟\mathcal{D}. If it was (II), then only the width of the last rectangle in 𝒟\mathcal{D} changes while its heights stays the same, so (iii) holds for 𝒟\mathcal{D}. If the last operation was (III) and the number of rectangles in 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} increases, then the location of the bottom of the last rectangle in 𝒟\mathcal{D} strictly increases, which ensures that property (a) and (b) in point (iii) cannot hold simultaneously with R3R_{3} as this last rectangle. Finally, if the last operation is (IV), then in the non-trivial case, 𝒟\mathcal{D} has one more rectangle than 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} but this rectangle has the same bottom as the last rectangle in 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} so (c) does not hold.

(i​i​i)⟹(i)(iii)\implies(i) Suppose λ/μ\lambda/\mu contains 332/1332/1. We must show that there are three consecutive rectangles in the rectangular decomposition of λ/μ\lambda/\mu such that (a), (b), (c) hold for these.

Since λ/μ\lambda/\mu contains 332/1332/1 as a subshape, we can then find an inner corner (i1,j1)(i_{1},j_{1}) and an outer corner (i2,j2)(i_{2},j_{2}) of λ/μ\lambda/\mu such that the subshape of λ/μ\lambda/\mu consisting of rows i1i_{1} to i2i_{2} and columns j1+1j_{1}+1 to j2−1j_{2}-1 is a rectangle; call this R2R_{2}. Then if R1R_{1} is the rectangle consisting of column j1j_{1} and R3R_{3} is the rectangle consisting of column j2j_{2}, it is clear that rectangles R1,R2,R3R_{1},R_{2},R_{3} satisfy properties (a), (b), (c). See Figure 9 for an example of this on 332/1332/1 itself. This concludes the proof. ∎

We now introduce a tool that will give us a way to correspond between rook placements and lattice paths. The idea is to represent a lattice path by a permutation the ithi^{\textnormal{th}} entry of which keeps track of which row or column index of the skew shape the ithi^{\textnormal{th}} step of the lattice path occupies, as counted from the bottom.

Definition 3.15 (Path permutation).

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape with rr rows and cc columns labeled in the usual way. The path permutation corresponding to LL is ψL=ψ1​…​ψr+c∈𝔖r+c\psi_{L}=\psi_{1}\ldots\psi_{r+c}\in\mathfrak{S}_{r+c} as below:

ψi={column index of the column occupied by step iif i is an East step,row index of the row occupied by step iif i is a North step.\psi_{i}=\begin{cases}\text{column index of the column occupied by step $i$}\quad&\text{if $i$ is an East step,}\\ \text{row index of the row occupied by step $i$}\quad&\text{if $i$ is a North step.}\end{cases}
Example 3.16.

Consider the blue lattice path LL drawn in the figure below:

Then the corresponding path permutation is given (in 2-line notation) as

ψL=[12345678910111213148765941031121213141].\psi_{L}=\left[\begin{array}[]{cccccccccccccc}\scriptstyle{1}&\scriptstyle{2}&\scriptstyle{3}&\scriptstyle{4}&\scriptstyle{5}&\scriptstyle{6}&\scriptstyle{7}&\scriptstyle{8}&\scriptstyle{9}&\scriptstyle{10}&\scriptstyle{11}&\scriptstyle{12}&\scriptstyle{13}&\scriptstyle{14}\\ \scriptstyle{8}&\scriptstyle{7}&\scriptstyle{6}&\scriptstyle{5}&\scriptstyle{9}&\scriptstyle{4}&\scriptstyle{10}&\scriptstyle{3}&\scriptstyle{11}&\scriptstyle{2}&\scriptstyle{12}&\scriptstyle{13}&\scriptstyle{14}&\scriptstyle{1}\end{array}\right].

Below, we define a very special lattice path inside λ/μ\lambda/\mu that only exists when λ/μ\lambda/\mu is 332/1332/1-avoiding. The permutation corresponding to this path turns out to be precisely the bijection that will induce the matroid isomorphism between 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} and ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} shown ahead. In Section 5, the skew shape is given a different labeling; the path permutation with respect to this labeling plays a crucial ingredient in the proof of the main result in that section.

Definition 3.17 (Spine path).

Suppose that λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a 332/1332/1-avoiding skew shape contained in an r×cr\times c rectangle. Let R1,…,RkR_{1},\dotsc,R_{k} denote the rectangles in the rectangular decomposition of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. (Note that these rectangles satisfy item (iii) in Proposition 3.14.) We construct a lattice path LL of length r+cr+c as follows.

Start from the lower left hand corner of R1R_{1}.

  1. (i)

    If there is only one rectangle (k=1)(k=1) then let LL be the North–East boundary of R1R_{1}.

  2. (ii)

    If the bottom of R2R_{2} is not at the same level as the bottom of R1R_{1}, take North steps until the bottom of R2R_{2} is reached, and then East steps until the lower left corner of R2R_{2} is reached. Recursively construct the rest of LL from here based on the shape R2,R3,…,RkR_{2},R_{3},\dotsc,R_{k}.

  3. (iii)

    If k≥3k\geq 3, and if the bottom of R1R_{1} and R2R_{2} are the same, and the top of R1R_{1} is at the same level as the bottom of R3R_{3}, then take North steps until the top of R1R_{1} is reached, and then take East steps until the bottom left corner of R3R_{3} is reached. Recursively construct the rest of LL based on the shape R3,…,RkR_{3},\dotsc,R_{k}.

  4. (iv)

    In any other case, follow the North–East border of R1R_{1}. This ends somewhere on the left side of R2R_{2}, say at (p,q)(p,q). Now construct the rest of LL using the part of the shape which is North–East of (p,q)(p,q).

    Observe that we apply this case if (a) k=2k=2, (b) the bottoms of R1R_{1}, R2R_{2} and R3R_{3} are the same, or (c) when the bottom of R3R_{3} is strictly above the top of R2R_{2}.

    (Observe, the case when the bottom of R3R_{3} is strictly below the top of R1R_{1} does not appear, since this would violate the 332/1332/1-avoiding property, see Proposition 3.14, so we have covered all cases.)

See Figure 10 for an illustration of the four cases.

The resulting lattice path is called the spine path of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. By definition, the spine path is always contained inside λ/μ\lambda/\mu.

Example 3.18.

The spine path is particularly easy to construct for Ferrers shapes, see the first shape in Figure 11.

Below, when we refer to a North-East segment of LL, we mean the word 𝙽𝙴\mathtt{NE} as a subword of LL when written as a sequence of 𝙽\mathtt{N}s and 𝙴\mathtt{E}s.

Lemma 3.19.

Suppose LL is the spine path of a 332/1332/1-avoiding skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu, and consider a corner of the spine path formed by a North-East segment of LL occuring in row pp and column qq of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Then the subshape {(i,j)∈λ/μ:i≥p,j≥q}\{(i,j)\in\lambda/\mu:i\geq p,j\geq q\} of λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a rectangle.

Similarly, if an East–North corner of LL occurs in column qq and row pp, then the subshape {(i,j)∈λ/μ:i≤p,j≤q}\{(i,j)\in\lambda/\mu:i\leq p,j\leq q\} of λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a rectangle.

Remark 3.20.

See Figure 11 for an example of this property. The idea behind this lemma is that no run of East steps of the spine path intersects the interior of more than one rectangle in the skew shape.

Proof.

We only prove the statement concerning the North-East segments of LL since the other case can be proved analogously. Let R1,…,RkR_{1},\dotsc,R_{k} be the rectangles in the rectangular decomposition of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. We note that each rectangle in the rectangle decomposition of a skew shape can contain at most one subshape induced by a North-East segment; this is because any run of East steps of the spine path intersects the interior of at most one rectangle in the skew shape. Let D1,…,DkD_{1},\ldots,D_{k} be these (possibly empty) Ferrers shapes. If there is indeed a 𝙽𝙴\mathtt{NE} segment of LL in RiR_{i}, we will call DiD_{i} non-degenerate.

We proceed by induction on kk. When k=1k=1, λ/μ\lambda/\mu is itself a rectangle and LL is, by construction, the North-East boundary of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Hence the subshape formed by the only North-East segment of LL is also a rectangle.

If k=2k=2 or 33, the result follows by a casewise inspection of the relative heights of the rectangles R1,R2,R3R_{1},R_{2},R_{3} and the construction of the spine path in Definition 3.17.

Suppose now k>3k>3 and the result holds for all skew shapes with at most k−1k-1 rectangles in the rectangle decomposition. Let LL be the spine path of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. By construction of LL, the restriction of LL to the rectangles R1,…,Rk−3R_{1},\ldots,R_{k-3} is the spine path L′L^{\prime} of the skew shape with rectangular decomposition R1,…,Rk−3R_{1},\ldots,R_{k-3}. Applying the induction hypothesis to this skew shape and L′L^{\prime}, we see that each of D1,…,Dk−3D_{1},\ldots,D_{k-3} is a rectangle.

It remains to consider DiD_{i} for i=k−2,k−1i=k-2,k-1 and kk. If Dk−2D_{k-2} is non-degenerate, one of two cases can occur: (a) LL crosses the interior of Rk−2R_{k-2}. This corresponds to case (ii) in the spine path construction and hence Dk−2D_{k-2} is clearly a rectangle; or else we have (b) LL does not cross the interior of Rk−2R_{k-2}, in which instance either case (iii) or (iv) from the spine path construction holds. In each of these cases, the rectangle(s) succeeding Rk−2R_{k-2} have the same bottom as Rk−2R_{k-2} so once again Dk−2D_{k-2} is a rectangle. If Dk−1D_{k-1} is non-degenerate, only cases (ii) and (iv a) of the spine path construction can occur; in both cases it is immediate that Dk−1D_{k-1} is a rectangle. Finally by construction of the spine path, LL travels along the North-East boundary of RkR_{k} and hence DkD_{k} equals RkR_{k} itself and is hence a rectangle. ∎

For brevity, let ψλ/μ\psi_{\lambda/\mu} be the path permutation determined by the spine path of λ/μ\lambda/\mu whenever λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a 332/1332/1-avoiding skew shape. This is called the spine bijection for short. We will show that if λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a 332/1332/1-avoiding skew shape then its spine bijection induces a bijection from the bases of 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} to the bases of ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}. By an abuse of notation, we call the induced map between set systems ψλ/μ\psi_{\lambda/\mu}. Note that the spine bijection sends the basis in 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} corresponding to the spine path to the non-nesting rook placement in ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} without any rooks. Before proceeding with the proof, we first give an example.

We can see by inspection that ψλ\psi_{\lambda} induces a bijection from lattice paths in 𝒫321\mathcal{P}_{321} to non-nesting rook placements in ℛ321\mathcal{R}_{321}. We illustrate the induced bijection ψ321:𝒫321→ℛ321\psi_{321}:\mathcal{P}_{321}\to\mathcal{R}_{321} below by drawing the lattice paths together with the corresponding non-nesting rook placements. Each shape is labeled with the lattice path basis on the left and its corresponding non-nesting rook placement basis on the right.

      
      

A crucial ingredient in generalizing the idea above is the presence of a spine path, which we know can only be defined in 332/1332/1-avoiding shapes. The following theorem shows that a rook matroid and lattice path matroid on the same skew Ferrers shape are isomorphic if and only if 332/1332/1 does not occur as a subshape of λ/μ\lambda/\mu.

Before we prove this, we introduce a definition that allows one to move between lattice paths contained inside a skew shape.

Definition 3.22.

Two lattice paths LL and L′L^{\prime} are related by a flip if LL can be obtained from L′L^{\prime} by either (a) flipping an East-North segment of L′L^{\prime} to a North-East segment, or (b) flipping a North-East segment to an East-North segment.

We are now ready to state the main theorem of this subsection.

Theorem 3.23.

The lattice path matroid 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} is isomorphic to the non-nesting rook matroid ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} if and only if λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a 332/1332/1-avoiding skew shape. In that case, an explicit bijection from 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} to ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} is given by ψλ/μ\psi_{\lambda/\mu}.

Proof.

For the only if direction: suppose λ/μ\lambda/\mu contains 332/1332/1 as a subshape, then ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} would contain Q6Q_{6} as a minor by Lemma 3.9 and Lemma 3.7. But Q6Q_{6} is an excluded minor (see [Bon10, Thm. 3.1]) for the class of lattice path matroids so ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} cannot be isomorphic to 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu}.

For the if direction: Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a 332/1332/1-avoiding skew shape on rr rows and cc columns. Since λ/μ\lambda/\mu avoids 332/1332/1, we can consider its spine path L0L_{0} and the associated spine bijection ψλ/μ\psi_{\lambda/\mu}, which for the purpose of brevity we occasionally refer to as ψ\psi. Recall that we are identifying a lattice path by its set of East steps.

In the two-line notation of the spine path permutation, we partition the columns into blocks, formed by runs of steps in the same direction (North or East). We then circle the East steps of the spine path.

Since ψλ/μ\psi_{\lambda/\mu} is a bijection from [r+c][r+c] to itself, the result will follow if we can show that ψλ/μ\psi_{\lambda/\mu} maps lattice paths inside λ/μ\lambda/\mu to non-nesting rook placements on λ/μ\lambda/\mu. To that end, we make the following claim.

Claim: If LL is a lattice path contained inside λ/μ\lambda/\mu, then ψλ/μ​(L)\psi_{\lambda/\mu}(L) defines a non-nesting rook placement on λ/μ\lambda/\mu.

We prove the claim by induction on kk, the number of cells between LL and the spine path. For the k=0k=0 case, LL is the spine path itself, the East steps of which, by construction, correspond to the column indices of λ/μ\lambda/\mu which implies that ψλ/μ​(L0)\psi_{\lambda/\mu}(L_{0}) is the empty rook placement.

Now suppose k>1k>1 and consider any lattice path L+L^{+} contained inside λ/μ\lambda/\mu with kk cells between it and L0L_{0}. Then L+L^{+} can be obtained from some lattice path LL in λ/μ\lambda/\mu with k−1k-1 cells between LL and L0L_{0}, via a flip. In the two-line notation of ψλ/μ\psi_{\lambda/\mu}, circle the East steps of LL. By induction hypothesis, the values below the circled entries, ψλ/μ​(L)\psi_{\lambda/\mu}(L), defines a valid non-nesting rook placement ρL\rho_{L} on λ/μ\lambda/\mu. In the case of our example, this becomes:

Figure 12 illustrates this on our running example. At the level of the circled entries of the first line of ψλ/μ\psi_{\lambda/\mu}, the flipping of an 𝙴𝙽\mathtt{EN} segment to a 𝙽𝙴\mathtt{NE} segment or vice versa corresponds to moving a circle (the index of an East step) either one position left or right. In the running example, there are four such North-East segments and three East-North segments which can be flipped.

We will show that ψλ/μ​(L+)\psi_{\lambda/\mu}(L^{+}) is also a non-nesting rook placement contained within λ/μ\lambda/\mu. The set ψλ/μ​(L+)\psi_{\lambda/\mu}(L^{+}) certainly defines a non-nesting rook placement within the rectangle occupied by λ/μ\lambda/\mu. It remains to show that this rook placement has its rooks on λ/μ\lambda/\mu as well. By Lemma 3.19, we know that any such flip occurs in a rectangular region determined by the spine path. Note that such a rectangular region is given by row and column indices in two adjacent blocks in the two-line notation. For example, the fifth and sixth block in our example, corresponds to the rectangle in rows 1,2,31,2,3 and columns 13,1413,14.

Let ii and i+1i+1 be consecutive steps of the lattice path LL such that exactly one of them is an East step. (Recall that a circled index is an East step). Consider the row/column indices ψ⁡(i)\psi(i) and ψ⁡(i+1)\psi(i+1) and recall that we have partitioned the columns of the two-line array of the spine bijection ψλ/μ\psi_{\lambda/\mu} into blocks. There are four cases to consider:

  • A.

    ψ⁡(i)\psi(i) and ψ⁡(i+1)\psi(i+1) are both column indices from the same block.

  • B.

    ψ⁡(i)\psi(i) and ψ⁡(i+1)\psi(i+1) are both row indices from the same block.

  • C.

    ψ⁡(i)\psi(i) and ψ⁡(i+1)\psi(i+1) are in different blocks, and the East step (recall, exactly one of ii and i+1i+1) is mapped to a column index.

  • D.

    ψ⁡(i)\psi(i) and ψ⁡(i+1)\psi(i+1) are in different blocks, and the East step of LL is mapped to a row index.

These four cases appear in the black lattice path LL shown in Figure 12. We have a Case A flip for step i=4i=4, Case B for step i=1i=1, Case C for step i=9i=9 and Case D for step i=7i=7.

We now describe how a flip on a segment of LL affects the rook placement ρL\rho_{L} in each case. It is clear in each case that ψλ/μ​(L+)\psi_{\lambda/\mu}(L^{+}) is obtained from ψλ/μ​(L)\psi_{\lambda/\mu}(L) by swapping ψ⁡(i)\psi(i) or ψ⁡(i+1)\psi(i+1) for the other element. We will see that in every case this corresponds to moving the rooks of ρL\rho_{L} such that they still stay on λ/μ\lambda/\mu, since all operations are performed on some rectangle above or below the spine path as guaranteed by Lemma 3.19. We consider each of the cases above.

  • A.

    In this case we have two adjacent columns ψ⁡(i)\psi(i) and ψ⁡(i+1)\psi(i+1) where one is empty the other is occupied by a rook of ρL\rho_{L}. We can then move the rook horizontally to the adjacent column and obtain a new valid rook placement on λ/μ\lambda/\mu.

  • B.

    In this case we have two adjacent rows ψ⁡(i)\psi(i) and ψ⁡(i+1)\psi(i+1) where one is empty the other is occupied by a rook. The rook is moved vertically to the adjacent row to obtain a new new valid rook placement on λ/μ\lambda/\mu.

  • C.

    There are two sub-cases to consider.

    In the first case, we have an empty column p=ψ⁡(i)p=\psi(i) and an empty row q=ψ⁡(i+1)q=\psi(i+1) of ρL\rho_{L} and need to make22 2 In the two-line array, this corresponds to moving a circle one step to the right. both occupied without affecting the occupancy of the other rows or columns, or the non-nesting nature of the other rooks of ρL\rho_{L}.

    There are two configurations to consider. Either the rectangle North-West of the cell (q,p)(q,p) is empty, or it contains some rooks (marked with ∙\bullet). In the first case, we simply place a rook in (q,p)(q,p). This is shown in the figure on the left below.

We then move the rooks of ρL\rho_{L} to the the locations marked ∘\circ, once again obtaining a new valid non-nesting rook placement on λ/μ\lambda/\mu, without affecting the occupancy of any other row or column of ρL\rho_{L}.

Again, two configurations may arise: one where ρL\rho_{L} has a rook in (p,q)(p,q) and one where it does not. This situation is precisely the inverse of Case C:

This shows that ψλ/μ​(L+)\psi_{\lambda/\mu}(L^{+}) also defines a non-nesting rook placement on λ/μ\lambda/\mu, completing the proof of the claim. With this, the proof of the theorem follows since ψλ/μ:𝒫λ/μ→ℛλ/μ\psi_{\lambda/\mu}:\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu}\to\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} is a well-defined map between the collections of bases of two matroids that is induced by a bijection between their groundsets. ∎

Example 3.24.

We describe the results of performing the four types of flips in Figure 12. Recall that the lattice path LL is described by the indices of its East steps, L={2,4,7,9,11,12,13}L=\{2,4,7,9,11,12,13\}.

  • •
