Remark 3.25.

It would be of interest to find a matroidal proof of Theorem 3.23. One reason that this might be possible is that the isomorphism ℛλ≅𝒫λ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda}\cong\mathcal{P}_{\lambda} can be proven from a matroid theoretic perspective as follows: Ferrers shapes can be built from a single box, using top row duplication and single box addition; the former operation corresponds to free extension of a rook matroid by a single element and the latter corresponds to series extension of a rook matroid by a single element. A similar strategy would be to find the correct type of matroid extension that corresponds to operations (I)-(IV) in Proposition 3.14 (ii) for all 332/1332/1-avoiding shapes.

Theorem 3.23 gives us a single criterion for when a rook matroid is isomorphic to a lattice path matroid, in terms of avoiding a fixed subshape.

In a different direction, we can obtain lattice path matroids as contractions of large enough rook matroids, where the meaning of large enough is made precise in the following proposition.

Proposition 3.26.

Suppose λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a skew shape with rr rows. The lattice path matroid 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} is isomorphic to the contraction ℛλ∗/μ∗/[r]\mathcal{R}_{\lambda^{\ast}/\mu^{\ast}}/[r], i.e.

𝒫λ/μ≅ℛλ∗/μ∗/[r],\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu}\cong\mathcal{R}_{\lambda^{\ast}/\mu^{\ast}}/[r],

where

λ∗\displaystyle\lambda^{\ast} ≔(λ1+r,λ2+r−1,…,λr−1+2,λr+1),\displaystyle\coloneqq(\lambda_{1}+r,\lambda_{2}+r-1,\dotsc,\lambda_{r-1}+2,\lambda_{r}+1),
μ∗\displaystyle\mu^{\ast} ≔(μ1+r−1,μ2+r−2,…,μℓ+r−ℓ).\displaystyle\coloneqq(\mu_{1}+r-1,\mu_{2}+r-2,\dotsc,\mu_{\ell}+r-\ell).
Proof.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu have cc columns. Note that 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} and ℛλ∗/μ∗/[r]\mathcal{R}_{\lambda^{*}/\mu^{*}}/[r] are matroids on the ground sets [r+c][r+c] and [r+1,2​r+c][r+1,2r+c], respectively. Let f:[r+c]→[r+1,2​r+c]f:[r+c]\to[r+1,2r+c] be defined by f⁡(i)=i+rf(i)=i+r; then ff is clearly a bijection. It suffices to show that ff sends bases of 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} to bases of ℛλ∗/μ∗/[r]\mathcal{R}_{\lambda^{*}/\mu^{*}}/[r]. In other words, ff must send lattice paths contained in λ/μ\lambda/\mu to rook placements contained in λ∗/μ∗\lambda^{*}/\mu^{*} such that every row is occupied. The map ff modifies the lattice path LL in λ/μ\lambda/\mu to obtain a lattice path L′L^{\prime} in λ∗/μ∗\lambda^{*}/\mu^{*} such that every North step of LL becomes an East-North step of L′L^{\prime}. An example is shown in Figure 14. A rook is then placed in every outer corner of the path, and since we have one outer corner for each row, we are done. ∎

Rook matroids are shown to be positroids in Section 3.3, and positroids are known to be closed under taking minors [ARW16, Proposition 3.5] and under a cyclic shift of the groundset [ARW16, Lemma 3.3]. Since the map ff in the proof of Proposition 3.26 is a cyclic shift, we can thus deduce that every lattice path matroid is a positroid, a fact first proven in [Oh11].

The following corollary is immediate from Proposition 3.26.

Corollary 3.27.

Let λ\lambda be a partition of length ℓ\ell, and

λ⊳≔(λ1+ℓ,λ2+ℓ−1,…,λℓ−1+2,λℓ+1).\lambda^{\triangleright}\coloneqq(\lambda_{1}+\ell,\lambda_{2}+\ell-1,\dotsc,\lambda_{\ell-1}+2,\lambda_{\ell}+1).

We then have the following matroid isomorphism:

ℛλ≅ℛλ⊳/{1,2,…,ℓ}.\mathcal{R}_{\lambda}\cong\mathcal{R}_{\lambda^{\triangleright}}/\{1,2,\dotsc,\ell\}.

This also gives us a matroidal way to interpret maximal non-nesting rook placements on a Ferrers diagram and note that the matroid structure is the same as that of a Schubert matroid.

3.3. Relation to positroids

Definition 3.28.

Let AA be a d×nd\times n matrix with real entries such that all its maximal minors are non-negative. The representable matroid M⁡(A)M(A) associated to AA is called a positroid.

The property of being a positroid is strongly dependent on the total ordering on the ground set of the matroid. The assertions we make in this subsection depend on the ordering previously introduced on the ground set of the rook matroid; for convenience, we give this ordering a name.

Definition 3.29.

We say that a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu with rr rows and cc columns has the matroid labeling if its rows are labeled 11 to rr from top to bottom and the columns are labeled r+1r+1 to r+cr+c from left to right.

Throughout this subsection, every rook matroid will have the matroid labeling. This turns out to be the correct total ordering on the ground set in order for the rook matroid to be a positroid; the reason for this is hinted at when determining the Grassmann necklace of this matroid.

As alluded to before, there are several classes of combinatorial objects with which positroids are in bijection[Pos06]. The Grassmann necklaces make up one such class; we recall their definition below.

Definition 3.30.

Let d≤nd\leq n be positive integers. A Grassmann necklace of type (d,n)(d,n) is a sequence (I1,…,In)(I_{1},\ldots,I_{n}) of dd-subsets Ik∈([n]d)I_{k}\in\binom{[n]}{d} such that for any i∈[n]i\in[n],

  1. (1)

    If i∈Iii\in I_{i}, then Ii+1=Ii∖{i}∪{j}I_{i+1}=I_{i}\setminus\{i\}\cup\{j\} for some j∈[n]j\in[n].

  2. (2)

    If i∉Iii\notin I_{i}, then Ii+1=IiI_{i+1}=I_{i}, where In+1≔I1I_{n+1}\coloneqq I_{1}.

The ii-order on [n][n] is the total order defined by

i<ii+1<i…<in<i1<i…<ii−2<ii−1.i<_{i}i+1<_{i}\ldots<_{i}n<_{i}1<_{i}\ldots<_{i}i-2<_{i}i-1.

Fixing i∈[n]i\in[n], the Gale order with respect to <i<_{i} is the partial order on ([n]d)\binom{[n]}{d} defined by:

S≤iT⇔sj≤itjfor all j∈[d],S\leq_{i}T\iff s_{j}\leq_{i}t_{j}\quad\text{for all $j\in[d]$},

where S={s1<i…<isd}S=\{s_{1}<_{i}\ldots<_{i}s_{d}\} and T={t1<i…<itd}T=\{t_{1}<_{i}\ldots<_{i}t_{d}\} are ordered in the ii-order.

Grassmann necklaces arise naturally from matroids in the following way. Let M=([n],ℬ)M=([n],\mathcal{B}) be a matroid of rank dd and let IkI_{k} be the lexicographically minimal basis in ℬ\mathcal{B} with respect to <k<_{k}. Then ℐ⁡(M)=(I1,…,In)\mathcal{I}(M)=(I_{1},\ldots,I_{n}) is the Grassmann necklace of a matroid, from the following proposition.

Proposition 3.31.

[Pos06, Lemma 16.3] For any matroid M=([n],ℬ)M=([n],\mathcal{B}) of rank dd, ℐ⁡(M)\mathcal{I}(M) is a Grassmann necklace of type (d,n)(d,n).

Conversely, matroids—more specifically positroids—can be cooked up from Grassmann necklaces by the theorem below. This also yields necessary and sufficient criteria for a matroid to be a positroid in terms of Grassmann necklaces. This was first conjectured by [Pos06] who proved necessity; the sufficiency was proven by Oh [Oh11].

Theorem 3.32 ([Oh11, Pos06]).

Let ℐ=(I1,…,In)\mathcal{I}=(I_{1},\ldots,I_{n}) be a Grassmann necklace of type (r,n)(r,n) and let

B(ℐ)={B∈([n]r):B≥jIjfor all j∈[n]}.B(\mathcal{I})=\left\{B\in\binom{[n]}{r}:B\geq_{j}I_{j}\,\,\text{for all $j\in[n]$}\right\}.

Then M⁡(ℐ)=([n],B⁡(ℐ))M(\mathcal{I})=([n],B(\mathcal{I})) is a matroid of rank rr on [n][n] with collection of bases B⁡(ℐ)B(\mathcal{I}). Furthermore, if M=([n],ℬ)M=([n],\mathcal{B}) is a matroid with Grassmann necklace ℐ=ℐ⁡(M)\mathcal{I}=\mathcal{I}(M), then ℬ⊆B⁡(ℐ)\mathcal{B}\subseteq B(\mathcal{I}), with equality holding if and only MM is a positroid.

With this background in place, we make the following definition to distinguish certain non-nesting rook placements.

Definition 3.33.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape with rr rows and cc columns. For i∈[r+c]i\in[r+c], the ii-extremal non-nesting rook placement on λ/μ\lambda/\mu is the rook placement obtained by the following procedure.

If i∈[1,r]i\in[1,r]:

  1. (1)

    Place a rook in the last cell of row ii.

  2. (2)

    For j∈[i+1,r]j\in[i+1,r], place a rook in row jj as far to the right as possible, while ensuring the non-nesting condition holds.

If i∈[r+1,r+c]i\in[r+1,r+c]:

  1. (1)

    For j∈[i,r+c]j\in[i,r+c], leave column jj unoccupied.

  2. (2)

    For j∈[1,r]j\in[1,r], place a rook in row jj as far to the right as possible while maintaining the unoccupied status of the columns in steps (1)(1).

The resulting rook placement is non-nesting since the non-nesting condition is maintained at every step. An example is illustrated in Figure 15. The name is justified by the following lemma which characterises Grassmann necklaces of rook matroids in terms of extremal rook placements.

Proposition 3.34.

Let ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} be the rook matroid on skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Let ℐ=(I1,…,Ir+c)\mathcal{I}=(I_{1},\ldots,I_{r+c}) be the associated Grassmann necklace. Then for each i∈[r+c]i\in[r+c], IiI_{i} is the ii-extremal non-nesting rook placement on λ/μ\lambda/\mu.

Proof.

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be the collection of bases of ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}. Fix i∈[r+c]i\in[r+c]. By definition, IiI_{i} is the lexicographically minimal element in ℬ\mathcal{B} with respect to the ii-order <i<_{i}; let the corresponding non-nesting rook placement be τi\tau_{i}. Let the ii-extremal non-nesting rook placement on λ/μ\lambda/\mu be ρi\rho_{i}. Order the elements of IiI_{i} and R⁡(ρi)∪C⁡(ρi)R(\rho_{i})\cup C(\rho_{i}) in the ii-order as follows:

Ii=R⁡(τi)∪C⁡(τi)\displaystyle I_{i}=R(\tau_{i})\cup C(\tau_{i}) ={j1<ij2<i…<ijc},\displaystyle=\{j_{1}<_{i}j_{2}<_{i}\ldots<_{i}j_{c}\},
R⁡(ρi)∪C⁡(ρi)\displaystyle R(\rho_{i})\cup C(\rho_{i}) ={k1<ik2<i…<ikc}.\displaystyle=\{k_{1}<_{i}k_{2}<_{i}\ldots<_{i}k_{c}\}.

Claim: The equality Ii=R⁡(ρi)∪C⁡(ρi)I_{i}=R(\rho_{i})\cup C(\rho_{i}) holds.

We will prove that js=ksj_{s}=k_{s} by induction on ss. The s=1s=1 case is immediate since since k1=ik_{1}=i by construction and i≤ij1≤ik1i\leq_{i}j_{1}\leq_{i}k_{1}. Fix 2≤s≤c2\leq s\leq c and suppose j1=k1,…,js−1=ks−1j_{1}=k_{1},\ldots,j_{s-1}=k_{s-1}. Since i=j1<ijsi=j_{1}<_{i}j_{s}, we only consider the case when js∈[i,r+c]j_{s}\in[i,r+c] in the ii-order which coincides with the usual order on this interval; we will henceforth use << in place of <i<_{i}.

Suppose ii is a row index. Consider the element ks∈R⁡(ρi)∪C⁡(ρi)k_{s}\in R(\rho_{i})\cup C(\rho_{i}). Two cases arise:

Case 1: If ks≤rk_{s}\leq r, then ρi\rho_{i} has a rook as far to the right as possible in row ksk_{s} and by the procedure to generate extremal rook placements, there must necessarily be a rook in the row above; i.e. ks=ks−1+1.k_{s}=k_{s-1}+1. Putting this together with the induction hypothesis, we get that

js−1<js≤ks=ks−1+1=js−1+1,j_{s-1}<j_{s}\leq k_{s}=k_{s-1}+1=j_{s-1}+1,

so we must have equality between jsj_{s} and ksk_{s}.

Case 2: If ks≥r+1k_{s}\geq r+1, then column ksk_{s} is empty. If ks−1≥r+1k_{s-1}\geq r+1, then there is no rook in column ks−1k_{s-1} either. By the same reasoning as in Case 1, we must necessarily have js=ksj_{s}=k_{s}.

If ks−1≤rk_{s-1}\leq r then columns r+1r+1 to ks−1k_{s}-1 are occupied by a rook of ρi\rho_{i}. This means that jsj_{s} cannot equal any column index r+1,…​ks−1r+1,\ldots k_{s}-1, since τi\tau_{i} and ρi\rho_{i} have rooks in rows corresponding to the columns above. This also means that the rook of ρi\rho_{i} in column r+1r+1 occurs in row ks−1k_{s-1}. If jsj_{s} were to be a row index between ks−1+1k_{s-1}+1 and rr, then there would be two rooks of τi\tau_{i} in column r+1r+1, which is infeasible. Hence jsj_{s} is not equal to any index in the interval (in the usual order) [ks−1+1,ks−1][k_{s-1}+1,k_{s}-1]. By minimality, we must then have js=ksj_{s}=k_{s}, and this completes the proof for the case when ii is a row index.

When ii is a column index, the proof proceeds along similar lines. Assume 2≤s≤c2\leq s\leq c and k1=j1,…,ks−1=js−1k_{1}=j_{1},\ldots,k_{s-1}=j_{s-1} holds. Again, two cases arise:

Case 1: If ks≤r+ck_{s}\leq r+c, then column ksk_{s} is empty and by construction of ρi\rho_{i}, column ks−1k_{s-1} must also be empty and hence ks−1=ks−1k_{s-1}=k_{s}-1 which by the same reasoning used above implies that js=ksj_{s}=k_{s}.

Case 2: If ksk_{s} is a row index, then ρi\rho_{i} has a rook in row ksk_{s}. If ks−1k_{s-1} is also a row index, which by the procedure that defines extremal rook placements, again implies that ks−1=ks−1k_{s-1}=k_{s}-1, from which js=ksj_{s}=k_{s}. If, on the other hand, ks−1k_{s-1} is a column index, then by virtue of ksk_{s} being a row index and the definition of ρi\rho_{i}, it must be that ks−1=r+ck_{s-1}=r+c and the rook in row ksk_{s} is in column i−1i-1. If jsj_{s} were any row index between 11 and ks−1k_{s}-1 then τi\tau_{i}, and hence ρi\rho_{i}, would have a rook in some column between ii and r+cr+c, which contradicts the fact that these columns are unoccupied by construction. By minimality, we must then have js=ksj_{s}=k_{s}, thereby completing the proof. ∎

We will make use of the above characterization to prove that rook matroids are positroids.

Theorem 3.35.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape and ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} be the corresponding rook matroid. Then ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} is a positroid.

Proof.

We will use the criterion in Theorem 3.32. Let ℐ=(I1,…,Ir+c)\mathcal{I}=(I_{1},\ldots,I_{r+c}) be the Grassmann necklace of ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}. By Lemma 3.34, each IiI_{i} corresponds to the ii-extremal non-nesting rook placement on λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Consider B∈([r+c]c)B\in\binom{[r+c]}{c} satisfying B≥jIjB\geq_{j}I_{j} for all j∈[r+c]j\in[r+c], where ≥j\geq_{j} denotes the jthj^{\textnormal{th}} Gale order. We need to show that BB is a basis of ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}. Since BB is some cc-subset of [r+c][r+c], there is some non-nesting rook placement ρ\rho on the r×cr\times c rectangle such that B=R⁡(ρ)∪C⁡(ρ)B=R(\rho)\cup C(\rho). We will be done if we can show that ρ\rho lies within λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Suppose the rooks of ρ\rho occupy the cells (ki,ji)(k_{i},j_{i}), for i=1,…,mi=1,\ldots,m where k1<…<kmk_{1}<\ldots<k_{m}. For each i=1,…,mi=1,\ldots,m, consider the corresponding kik_{i}-extremal non-nesting rook placements Iki=R⁡(σi)∪C⁡(σi)I_{k_{i}}=R(\sigma_{i})\cup C(\sigma_{i}) and let (ki,ℓi)(k_{i},\ell_{i}) be the first rook of σi\sigma_{i} in the kik_{i}-order. Since ℓi\ell_{i} is the last cell in row kik_{i}, we need to show that ji≤ℓij_{i}\leq\ell_{i} for i=1,…,mi=1,\ldots,m. We will prove this one rook at a time. Suppose to the contrary that j1>ℓ1j_{1}>\ell_{1}.

Let the elements of Ik1I_{k_{1}} and BB be respectively ordered in the k1k_{1}-order as

Ik1\displaystyle I_{k_{1}} ={t1<k1t2<k1…<k1tc},\displaystyle=\{t_{1}<_{k_{1}}t_{2}<_{k_{1}}\ldots<_{k_{1}}t_{c}\},
B\displaystyle B ={k1<k1k2<k1…<k1kc}.\displaystyle=\{k_{1}<_{k_{1}}k_{2}<_{k_{1}}\ldots<_{k_{1}}k_{c}\}.

Since (k1,j1)(k_{1},j_{1}) contains a rook of ρ\rho, we must have j1∈Ik1j_{1}\in I_{k_{1}}, since by the definition of the k1k_{1}-extremal rook placement, all the rooks of σ1\sigma_{1} occur in the interval [k1,r][k_{1},r]. So j1=tnj_{1}=t_{n}, for some n∈[1,c]n\in[1,c].

Note that ℓ1\ell_{1} is the last occupied column of Ik1I_{k_{1}}, so there exists tqt_{q} such that [ℓ1+1,r+c]=[tq,tc]⊂Ik1[\ell_{1}+1,r+c]=[t_{q},t_{c}]\subset I_{k_{1}}. Also, the maximal element of BB in the k1k_{1}-order must necessarily be a column index, since otherwise we would have a rook in σ1\sigma_{1} with a row index smaller than k1k_{1}. Since B≥k1Ik1B\geq_{k_{1}}I_{k_{1}}, we must have ki≥k1tik_{i}\geq_{k_{1}}t_{i} for i∈[q,c]i\in[q,c]. Since the elements on both sides of the inequality are column indices, the previous inequality also holds in the usual order. Then the sequence (ti)i=qc(t_{i})_{i=q}^{c} forms an interval of column indices terminating at the last column r+cr+c so we must necessarily have ki=tik_{i}=t_{i} for i∈[q,c]i\in[q,c]. Since j1>ℓ1=tqj_{1}>\ell_{1}=t_{q}, this implies in particular that kn=tn=j1k_{n}=t_{n}=j_{1}. Then j1∈Bj_{1}\in B, contradicting the fact that ρ\rho has a rook in (k1,j1)(k_{1},j_{1}). Thus j1≤ℓ1j_{1}\leq\ell_{1}.

Now consider (k2,j2)(k_{2},j_{2}); if j2>ℓ2j_{2}>\ell_{2} then by similar reasoning as above, we must have j2∈Ik2j_{2}\in I_{k_{2}}. Also note that the maximal element of BB in the k2k_{2}-order is k1k_{1}. Since ℓ2\ell_{2} is the last occupied column index of σ2\sigma_{2}, the interval [ℓ2+1,r+c][\ell_{2}+1,r+c] is a subset of Ik2I_{k_{2}}, forming its last r+c−ℓ2r+c-\ell_{2} elements in the k2k_{2} order. Let the column indices of ρ\rho corresponding to ℓ2+1,…,r+c−1\ell_{2}+1,\ldots,r+c-1 in the k2k_{2}-order be ks+1,…,ks+r+c−ℓ2−1k_{s+1},\ldots,k_{s+r+c-\ell_{2}-1}. Since B≥k2Ik2B\geq_{k_{2}}I_{k_{2}}, all of these column indices must take distinct values in the interval [ℓ2+1,r+c][\ell_{2}+1,r+c] but cannot take on the values j1j_{1} or j2j_{2}, since ρ\rho has a rook in these columns. Thus r+c−ℓ2−1r+c-\ell_{2}-1 indices have a total of r+c−ℓ2−2r+c-\ell_{2}-2 values to take on, which is impossible, since the elements of BB are distinct. We must hence have j2≤ℓ2j_{2}\leq\ell_{2}. An example is illustrated in Figure 16. Repeating this argument for the remaining row indices k3,…,kmk_{3},\ldots,k_{m} of ρ\rho, we see that each corresponding column index jij_{i} satisfies ji≤ℓij_{i}\leq\ell_{i}, which completes the proof. ∎

3.4. Tutte polynomials

In this subsection, we show that the Tutte polynomials of rook matroids and lattice path matroids coincide, thereby tightening the correspondence between these classes of matroids. This fact is not obvious a priori, given the fact that, from Theorem 3.23, lattice path matroids and rook matroids are not always isomorphic.

The Tutte polynomial is defined as the corank-nullity generating function of the matroid MM:

TM​(x,y)≔∑A⊆E(x−1)r⁡(E)−r⁡(A)​(y−1)|A|−r⁡(A).{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}T_{M}(x,y)}\coloneqq\sum_{A\subseteq E}(x-1)^{r(E)-r(A)}(y-1)^{|A|-r(A)}.

For an overview of results on Tutte polynomials, see [EMM22]. The important fact about Tutte polynomials that we will use is that it satisfies the deletion-contraction recursion:

(3) TM​(x,y)=TM/e​(x,y)+TM∖e​(x,y),T_{M}(x,y)=T_{M/e}(x,y)+T_{M\setminus e}(x,y),

where e∈Ee\in E is neither a loop nor a coloop.

In order to prove the stated equality of Tutte polynomials, we need the following simple lemma.

Lemma 3.36.

Let MM be a rook matroid on a skew shape with rr rows and cc columns. Then the two contractions M/rM/r and M/(r+1)M/(r+1) are isomorphic, and thus have the same Tutte polynomial.

Proof.

Bases of M/rM/r correspond to rook placements with a rook in the last row of the skew shape and bases of M/(r+1)M/(r+1) correspond to rook placements with no rook in the first column of the skew shape. Let f:[r+c]∖r→[r+c]∖(r+1)f:[r+c]\setminus r\to[r+c]\setminus(r+1) be defined by f⁡(i)=if(i)=i, for i≠r+1i\neq r+1 and f⁡(r+1)=rf(r+1)=r. Then ff is a bijection that sends bases of M/rM/r to bases of M/(r+1)M/(r+1): a rook placement with a rook in the cell (r,r+1)(r,r+1) gets mapped to itself while rook placements with empty first column and occupied row rr gets mapped to the rook placement obtained by moving the rook in row rr to the cell (r,r+1)(r,r+1). This movement does not affect the non-nesting nature of the rest of the rook placement. ∎

The following is a curious result, since we know that 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} and ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} are not isomorphic when λ/μ\lambda/\mu contains 332/1332/1 as a subshape. For the purpose of readability, we use T⁡(M,x,y)T(M;x,y) in place of TM​(x,y)T_{M}(x,y) ahead.

Theorem 3.37.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape. Then

T⁡(𝒫λ/μ,x,y)=T⁡(ℛλ/μ,x,y).T(\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu};x,y)=T(\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu};x,y).
Proof.

We proceed by induction over λ/μ\lambda/\mu, the number of squares in the diagram of the skew shape. The base case is immediate since both the lattice path matroid and the rook matroid on a singe square are equal to the uniform matroid U1,2U_{1,2}.

In D′D^{\prime} we have removed the first column of DD, in D′′D^{\prime\prime} we have removed the last row of DD, indexed by rr. The last picture indicates that the last row contains a rook.

The Tutte polynomial for the lattice path matroid satisfies

(4) T⁡(𝒫D,x,y)=T⁡(𝒫D′,x,y)+T⁡(𝒫D′′,x,y),T(\mathcal{P}_{D};x,y)=T(\mathcal{P}_{D^{\prime}};x,y)+T(\mathcal{P}_{D^{\prime\prime}};x,y),

by deletion-contraction, which corresponds to conditioning on whether or not the first step in the path is an East step or a North step.

Similarly, the Tutte polynomials for the rook matroid satisfies

(5) T⁡(ℛD,x,y)=T⁡(ℛD/r,x,y)+T⁡(ℛD′′,x,y),T(\mathcal{R}_{D};x,y)=T(\mathcal{R}_{D}/r;x,y)+T(\mathcal{R}_{D^{\prime\prime}};x,y),

by considering deletion-contraction of the last row index. By Lemma 3.36, we know that T⁡(ℛD/r,x,y)=T⁡(ℛD/(r+1),x,y)T(\mathcal{R}_{D}/r;x,y)=T(\mathcal{R}_{D}/(r+1);x,y) = T⁡(ℛD′,x,y)T(\mathcal{R}_{D^{\prime}};x,y) . By the induction hypothesis, we have that

T⁡(𝒫D′′,x,y)=T⁡(ℛD′′,x,y)​ and ​T​(𝒫D′,x,y)=T⁡(ℛD′,x,y).T(\mathcal{P}_{D^{\prime\prime}};x,y)=T(\mathcal{R}_{D^{\prime\prime}};x,y)\text{ and }T(\mathcal{P}_{D^{\prime}};x,y)=T(\mathcal{R}_{D^{\prime}};x,y).

Putting these all together, it follows that T⁡(𝒫D,x,y)=T⁡(ℛD,x,y)T(\mathcal{P}_{D};x,y)=T(\mathcal{R}_{D};x,y). ∎

The strongest form of the Merino-Welsh conjecture, formulated in [MW99], is a log-convexity type statement for evaluations of the Tutte polynomial; it says that if MM is a loopless and coloopless matroid then TM​(2,0)⋅TM​(0,2)≥TM​(1,1)2T_{M}(2,0)\cdot T_{M}(0,2)\geq T_{M}(1,1)^{2}. While recently disproved for general matroids [BCCP24], it has been shown to hold for certain classes of matroids including split matroids [FS23] and lattice path matroids [KMSRA18]. In the light of the latter result, Theorem 3.37 shows that this conjecture also holds for rook matroids.

Corollary 3.38.

Rook matroids satisfy the Merino–Welsh conjecture.

The Tutte polynomial is a valuative invariant of a matroid: it behaves well under subdivisions of matroid polytopes. On the basis of Theorem 3.37 and computer experiments, we make the case that every valuative invariant has the same value on ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} as it does on 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu}.

Conjecture 3.39.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape and let ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} and 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} be the corresponding rook matroid and lattice path matroid respectively. Then for every valuative invariant ff for matroids, we have

f⁡(ℛλ/μ)=f⁡(𝒫λ/μ).f(\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu})=f(\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu}).

In particular, the same would hold for a universal valuative invariant like Derksen’s 𝒢\mathcal{G}-invariant [Der09, DF10]. For a systematic treatment of valuative invariants of matroids, see [FS24].

4. Distributional properties of non-nesting rook numbers

In this section, we deduce the distributional properties of the coefficients of the non-nesting rook polynomial, using the underlying matroid structure.

4.1. Ultra-log-concavity of Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu}

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape with rr rows and cc columns. The basis-generating polynomial rλ/μr_{\lambda/\mu} of ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu} serves as the appropriate multivariate generalization of Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu}, the univariate non-nesting rook polynomial introduced in Section 2.1. To emphasize the role played by row and column variables separately – which will also be useful in Section 5 – we use 𝐱=(x1,…,xr)\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}) and 𝐲=(yr+1,…,yr+c)\mathbf{y}=(y_{r+1},\ldots,y_{r+c}) for the row and column variables of rλ/μr_{\lambda/\mu} respectively. By Theorem 3.3, bases of rook matroids correspond to occupied row indices taken together with unoccupied column indices of rook placements; we can thus write

(6) rλ/μ​(𝐱,𝐲)=∑ρ∈NNλ/μ∏i∈R⁡(ρ)xi​∏j∈C⁡(ρ)yj,r_{\lambda/\mu}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\sum_{\rho\in\text{NN}_{\lambda/\mu}}\prod_{i\in R(\rho)}x_{i}\prod_{j\in C(\rho)}y_{j},

where as before NNλ/μ\text{NN}_{\lambda/\mu} denotes the set of non-nesting rook placements on λ/μ\lambda/\mu and R⁡(ρ),C⁡(ρ)R(\rho),C(\rho) correspond to the set of row indices occupied by ρ\rho and the set of column indices that are not occupied by ρ\rho respectively.

The following theorem, proven by Stanley in 1981 for regular matroids and extended by Yan in 2023 to all matroids, is the larger setting within which we can view the ultra-log-concavity of the non-nesting rook numbers. For completeness, we reproduce the proof from [Yan23].

Theorem 4.1.

([Sta81, Theorem 2.1] and [Yan23, Corollary 3.47]) Let M=(E,ℬ)M=(E,\mathcal{B}) be a matroid of rank nn and let T⊆ET\subseteq E be some fixed subset of the ground set EE. If fi=#⁡{B∈ℬ:|B∩T|=i}f_{i}=\#\{B\in\mathcal{B}:|B\cap T|=i\}, then (fi)i=0n(f_{i})_{i=0}^{n} is ultra-log-concave with no internal zeros.

Proof.

The polynomial f⁡(t,s)=∑i=0nfi​ti​sn−if(t,s)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}f_{i}t^{i}s^{n-i} can be obtained by f⁡(t,s)=PM​(t⋅𝟏T+s⋅𝟏Tc)f(t,s)=P_{M}(t\cdot\mathbf{1}_{T}+s\cdot\mathbf{1}_{T^{c}}) where 𝟏T\mathbf{1}_{T} is the characteristic vector of TT. The result then follows from the fact that PMP_{M} is Lorentzian, specializing variables preserves Lorentzianness and a homogeneous bivariate polynomial is Lorentzian if and only if its coefficient sequence is ultra-log-concave with no internal zeros. ∎

This inequality is one of many arising in the framework of convex geometry and matroid theory that have been investigated from the perspective of characterizing equality conditions [CP24, vHYZ24]. For now, we note the immediate enumerative corollary relevant to us.

Corollary 4.2.

For every skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu, the coefficient sequence of the non-nesting rook polynomial Mλ/μ​(t)=∑k=0drk​(λ/μ)​tkM_{\lambda/\mu}(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}r_{k}(\lambda/\mu)t^{k} is ultra-log-concave with no internal zeros. That is,

(rk(dk))2≥rk−1(dk−1)⋅rk+1(dk+1)for all 1≤k≤d−1,\left(\dfrac{r_{k}}{\binom{d}{k}}\right)^{2}\geq\dfrac{r_{k-1}}{\binom{d}{k-1}}\cdot\dfrac{r_{k+1}}{\binom{d}{k+1}}\quad\text{for all $1\leq k\leq d-1$},

where dd is the degree of Mλ/μ​(t)M_{\lambda/\mu}(t).

Proof.

The conclusion follows from Theorem 4.1 applied to the rook matroid ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}, where T=[r]T=[r], the set of row indices of the skew shape. ∎

At this juncture, we note the parallel between the non-nesting rook polynomial and the full rook polynomial: both are ultra-log-concave. We will see that this is essentially the strongest property we can hope for, as it turns out that unlike the full rook polynomial the non-nesting counterpart is not real-rooted. We will show this in Section 5.2, where the proper context of this failure of real-rootedness is given. The relevance of the Stanley-Yan inequality to a different conjecture, namely Brenti’s log-concavity conjecture 5.2, will be made clear in Remark 5.11. For the moment, we approach the real-rootedness question via stability.

4.2. Lattice path matroids are not HPP

In the previous subsection, we saw that ultra-log-concavity holds for the non-nesting rook numbers. In this subsection, we probe the extent to which real-rootedness holds, using the framework of matroids with the half-plane property.

A robust necessary condition that a homogeneous, multiaffine polynomial is stable is that its support forms the collection of bases of a matroid [COSW04]. The half-plane property (HPP) of a matroid MM identifies whether the converse is true, namely that the basis-generating polynomial of M=(E,ℬ)M=(E,\mathcal{B}) defined as

PM​(𝐱)=∑B∈ℬ∏i∈Bxi,P_{M}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}}\prod_{i\in B}x_{i},

is stable. We call such a matroid HPP. In [COSW04], an in-depth investigation of the half-plane property for matroids was carried out. One question raised – a “wild speculation” according to [COSW04] – was if transversal matroids have the HPP. Shortly thereafter, Choe and Wagner provided an example of a rank 44 transversal matroid on 1212 elements that was not HPP [CW06]. Their example, however, is not a lattice path matroid; this can be straightforwardly checked using a criterion described in [BdM06, Theorem 3.14]. To our knowledge, the question of whether lattice path matroids have the HPP is thus still open. The purpose of this subsection is to give the first example of a lattice path matroid—in fact a Catalan matroid—that does not have the half-plane property.

Theorem 4.3.

There exists a generalized Catalan matroid that is not HPP. Concretely, the basis-generating polynomial of the matroid ℛλ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda} for λ=666333\lambda=666333 is not stable.

Proof.

Let λ=666333\lambda=666333 and P⁡(𝐱,𝐲)P(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) be the basis-generating polynomial of ℛλ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda}. It suffices to show that the univariate polynomial obtained from P⁡(𝐱,𝐲)P(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) obtained by setting some variables to tt and others to 11 is not real-rooted. Consider the univariate polynomial f⁡(t)=P⁡(𝐱,𝐲)f(t)=P(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) obtained by the substitution x1=x2=x3=y10=y11=y12=tx_{1}=x_{2}=x_{3}=y_{10}=y_{11}=y_{12}=t and x4=x5=x6=y7=y8=y9=1.x_{4}=x_{5}=x_{6}=y_{7}=y_{8}=y_{9}=1. Using SageMath, we found that

f⁡(t)=t6+36​t5+225​t4+400​t3.f(t)=t^{6}+36t^{5}+225t^{4}+400t^{3}.

This polynomial was found to have non-real roots near −3.6855±0.6232​i.-3.6855\pm 0.6232i. ∎

Corollary 4.4.

The Catalan matroid M10M_{10} is not HPP. That is, the basis-generating polynomial of M10M_{10} is not stable.

Proof.

Every generalized Catalan matroid is a minor of a large enough Catalan matroid [BdM06, Theorem 4.2]. In particular, if M10M_{10} denotes the Catalan matroid of order 1010 (realizable as a rook matroid on a staircase shape of size 1010), and X={4,5,9,10},Y={14,15,19,20}X=\{4,5,9,10\},Y=\{14,15,19,20\}, then ℛ666333\mathcal{R}_{666333} is isomorphic to M10\X/YM_{10}\backslash X/Y Lemma 3.7.

It follows that M10M_{10} cannot have the half-plane property. The rook matroid ℛ666333\mathcal{R}_{666333} cannot be obtained as a minor of M9M_{9}.

∎

Remark 4.5.

In [Xu15] it is stated that the class of generalized Catalan matroids is not HPP, however no explicit counterexample is given.

In [Mar16], it was shown that positroids have the Rayleigh property, a weaker property than having the half-plane property, which is known to be equivalent to being strongly Rayleigh [Brä07]. Since lattice path matroids are known to be positroids [Oh11], the results of this section complete the picture about half-plane properties of positroids.

4.3. Half-plane property of snake and panhandle matroids

We briefly turn our attention to two subclasses of lattice path matroids that satisfy the HPP – snake matroids and panhandle matroids – and give a direct proof of this using the Borcea-Brändén symbol theorem.

A skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu is called a snake44 4 Also known as ‘rim-hook’ or ‘border strip’. if it is connected and does not contain a 2×22\times 2-box of boxes. Lattice path matroids on such shapes are called snake matroids. Snake matroids are known to be graphic [KMSRA18, Theorem 3.2] and graphic matroids are HPP [Brä15, Section 9.1]. Our first goal is to prove the half-plane property of snake matroids without using the fact that snakes are graphic; next, we address the panhandle matroid case.

A priori, one reason to expect that snake matroids might satisfy the HPP is that the non-nesting rook polynomial on a snake is real-rooted. Indeed, the absence of 2×22\times 2 subshape implies that no configuration of rooks can be nesting, and hence the non-nesting rook polynomial on a snake is simply the regular rook polynomial and is thus real-rooted [Nij76].

If DD is the diagram of any skew shape, we can extend it by one box in one of two ways: by adding the box as a new column in the first row of DD or by adding it as a new row in the last column of DD. We denote these new diagrams by D→D_{\rightarrow} and D↑D_{\uparrow} respectively. We illustrate these constructions below for λ/μ=4331/21\lambda/\mu=4331/21.

Lemma 4.6.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape on rr rows and cc columns with diagram DD and let D→D_{\rightarrow} and D↑D_{\uparrow} be as over. Let PD​(𝐱,𝐲)P_{D}(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{y}) be the basis-generating polynomial for the rook matroid on λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Then the following recursions hold:

(7) PD→​(𝐱,𝐲)\displaystyle P_{D_{\rightarrow}}(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{y}) =yc+1​PD​(𝐱,𝐲)+x1​(PD​(𝐱,𝐲)|x1=0),\displaystyle=y_{c+1}P_{D}(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{y})+x_{1}\left(P_{D}(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{y})|_{x_{1}=0}\right),
(8) PD↑​(𝐱,𝐲)\displaystyle P_{D_{\uparrow}}(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{y}) =PD​(x2,…,xr+1,𝐲)+x1​∂∂yc​PD​(x2,…,xr+1,𝐲).\displaystyle=P_{D}(x_{2},\dotsc,x_{r+1};\mathbf{y})+x_{1}\frac{\partial}{\partial y_{c}}P_{D}(x_{2},\dotsc,x_{r+1};\mathbf{y}).
Proof.

Consider the deletion-contraction recurrence for the basis-generating polynomial of a matroid MM:

PM=PM∖e+xe⋅PM/e.P_{M}=P_{M\setminus e}+x_{e}\cdot P_{M/e}.

Equations (7) and (8) can be obtained from the above equation by taking M=ℛD→,e=r+c+1M=\mathcal{R}_{D_{\rightarrow}},e=r+c+1 and M=ℛD↑,e=1M=\mathcal{R}_{D_{\uparrow}},e=1 respectively. Alternatively, in each case the equations follow by conditioning on whether or not the new box contains a rook or not. ∎

Lemma 4.7.

Consider the linear operators T1T_{1} and T2T_{2} acting on multiaffine polynomials in the ring ℂ⁡[x1,…,xr+1,y1,…,yc+1]\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\dotsc,x_{r+1},y_{1},\dotsc,y_{c+1}] that are defined as

T1​[f]\displaystyle T_{1}[f] ≔yc+1​f+x1​(f|x1=0),\displaystyle\coloneqq y_{c+1}f+x_{1}\left(f|_{x_{1}=0}\right),
T2​[f]\displaystyle T_{2}[f] ≔f+xr+1​∂∂yc​f.\displaystyle\coloneqq f+x_{r+1}\frac{\partial}{\partial y_{c}}f.

Both T1T_{1} and T2T_{2} are stability preservers.

Proof.

We will use the Borcea-Brändén symbol theorem [BB09, Theorem 2.2]. Let

S=(x1+z1)​⋯​(xr+1+zr+1)​(y1+w1)​⋯​(yc+1+wc+1).S=(x_{1}+z_{1})\dotsm(x_{r+1}+z_{r+1})(y_{1}+w_{1})\dotsm(y_{c+1}+w_{c+1}).

Then T1T_{1} and T2T_{2} preserve stability if and only if the symbols T1​[S]T_{1}[S] and T2​[S]T_{2}[S] are stable as polynomials in the 𝐱,𝐲,𝐳,𝐰\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{z},\mathbf{w} variables. It then suffices to show that T1​[S]/ST_{1}[S]/S and T2​[S]/ST_{2}[S]/S are non-vanishing when all variables are in the upper half-plane. We have that

T1​[S]S=yc+1+(1x1+1z1)−1.\frac{T_{1}[S]}{S}=y_{c+1}+\left(\frac{1}{x_{1}}+\frac{1}{z_{1}}\right)^{-1}.

Since addition and inversion respectively preserve and flip the sign of the non-real part of a complex number lying in the upper half-plane, it is clear that the right-hand side lies in the upper-half-plane. Hence, T1T_{1} is stability-preserving. Similarly,

T2​[S]S=yc+wc+xr+1yc+wc\frac{T_{2}[S]}{S}=\frac{y_{c}+w_{c}+x_{r+1}}{y_{c}+w_{c}}

whose numerator is non-vanishing if all the variables have positive non-real part. So T2T_{2} is also stability-preserving. ∎

Note that the recursions (7) and (8) are, after a change of variables, represented by the operators T1T_{1} and T2T_{2} in Lemma 4.7. This lemma then gives us a recipe to establish the half-plane property of a lattice path matroid provided that it can be constructed from a smaller HPP matroid using →\rightarrow and ↑\uparrow. We use this below for snake and panhandle matroids.

Panhandle matroids are a simple class of lattice path matroids corresponding to Ferrers diagrams of the form (m,(n)a)(m,(n)^{a}), for m≥n≥1m\geq n\geq 1 and a≥1a\geq 1; the additional row of mm boxes on top of a n×an\times a rectangle suggests the name “panhandle”. This coinage was made in [HMM+23] where these matroids were studied in the context of their Ehrhart positivity. The proof we give here of the half-plane property of the panhandle matroids is similar in spirit to the original proof [COSW04]. Panhandle matroids can also be seen as series extensions of uniform matroids; taking series extensions preserves the HPP property in matroids by [COSW04, Proposition 4.10].

Proposition 4.8.

The following subclasses of lattice path matroids have the half-plane property:

  1. (1)

    Snake matroids.

  2. (2)

    Panhandle matroids.

Proof.

For (1), we proceed by induction on the number of boxes in the snake. In the case of one box we have that Pα​(𝐱,𝐲)=x1+y1P_{\alpha}(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{y})=x_{1}+y_{1}, which is stable. Since every snake can be built from one box by repeatedly performing the →\rightarrow and ↑\uparrow operations to the diagram, each of which preserves stability of the basis-generating polynomial, by Lemma 4.7, we are done.

For (2), we know that panhandle matroids are series extensions of uniform matroids. Since series extension of rook matroids corresponds to the →\rightarrow operation, we are done, since uniform matroids have the half-plane property and →\rightarrow preserves stability by Lemma 4.7. ∎

5. Rook placements as linear extensions

In this section, we make a bijective correspondence between labeled skew shapes and posets of width two. This allows us to provide an interpretation for the non-nesting rook polynomial in terms of a PP-Eulerian polynomial of a poset and deduce the following results among others. One, the PP-Eulerian polynomial of a width two poset is ultra-log-concave, thereby completing the picture of the Neggers–Stanley conjecture, which was disproved using a naturally labeled width two counterexample [Ste07]. We deduce this from a stronger statement, namely that a suitable multivariate analog of the PP-Eulerian polynomial—first considered in [BL16]—is Lorentzian. Returning to the rook polynomial setting, we learn that there exists a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu for which the non-nesting rook polynomial Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} has non-real roots. We end by considering the gamma-positivity properties of Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu}.

5.1. Neggers–Stanley conjecture

In this subsection we recall the statement and context of the Neggers–Stanley conjecture. For undefined terminology concerning posets, we refer to [Sta11].

Recall that given a poset PP, the width of PP is the size of the largest antichain in PP. A labeling of a poset PP on nn elements is a bijection ω:P→[n]\omega:P\to[n]. We say that ω\omega is a natural labeling, or linear extension of PP, if i≺ji\prec j implies ω⁡(i)<ω⁡(j).\omega(i)<\omega(j). The Jordan-Hölder set of (P,ω)(P,\omega) is the set of all permutations of [n][n] the inverses of which are linear extensions of (P,ω)(P,\omega) i.e., it is defined as

ℒ⁡(P,ω)={σ∈𝔖n:i≺j⟹σ−1​(ω⁡(i))<σ−1​(ω⁡(j))}.\mathcal{L}(P,\omega)=\{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}:i\prec j\implies\sigma^{-1}({\omega(i)})<\sigma^{-1}({\omega(j)})\}.

In other words, σ∈ℒ⁡(P)\sigma\in\mathcal{L}(P) if for every relation i≺ji\prec j in PP, we have that ω⁡(i)\omega(i) precedes ω⁡(j)\omega(j) in the one-line representation of the permutation σ.\sigma.

The (P,ω)(P,\omega)-Eulerian polynomial, also known as the WW-polynomial of PP, is the descent-generating polynomial of the Jordan-Hölder set of (P,ω)(P,\omega):

WP,ω​(t)=∑σ∈ℒ⁡(P,ω)tdes⁡(σ).W_{P,\omega}(t)=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{L}(P,\omega)}t^{\des(\sigma)}.

When ω\omega is natural, we simply write WPW_{P}, since the polynomial is independent of the choice of natural labeling. Observe that in the definitions of the multivariate analogs that follow, there is a dependence on the choice of natural labeling that we make explicit.

The distributional properties of WP,ωW_{P,\omega} was of early interest to combinatorialists working in poset theory. The following conjecture was first formulated by J. Neggers in 1978 for natural labelings ω\omega; in 1986, Stanley extended it to arbitrary labelings. Subsequent references to this conjecture also called it the Poset conjecture [Bre89]. For further background, the reader can consult [Brä15, Section 6].

Conjecture 5.1 (Neggers–Stanley conjecture [Neg78, Sta86]).

Let (P,ω)(P,\omega) be a labeled poset. Then WP,ωW_{P,\omega} is real-rooted.

The Neggers–Stanley conjecture was of central importance to algebraic combinatorics until its resolution in the negative in the early aughts: first by Brändén [Brä04a] who found a family of counterexamples to Stanley’s formulation and then Stembridge [Ste07] who disproved Neggers’ counterpart as well. In both cases, the counterexample furnished was of a width two poset; Brändén’s construction was non-naturally labeled while Stembridge’s (larger) counterexample was naturally labeled. Despite this breakthrough, the question of unimodality or log-concavity of WP,ωW_{P,\omega} for general (P,ω)(P,\omega) remained open. In particular, the following conjecture of Brenti has been open since 1989.

Conjecture 5.2.

[Bre89, Conjecture 1.1] Let (P,ω)(P,\omega) be a labeled poset. Then WP,ωW_{P,\omega} is log-concave with no internal zeroes.

There have been two positive results towards this end. V. Reiner and V. Welker proved that when PP is naturally labeled and graded, WPW_{P} is unimodal and symmetric [RW05]. Brändén then gave an elegant combinatorial proof of the same fact by demonstrating a stronger property: namely that WPW_{P} is γ\gamma-positive for the larger class of sign-graded posets [Brä06, Brä08].

In the next subsection, we show a strengthening of Conjecture 5.2 for special posets PP. Namely, we show that when PP is naturally labeled and of width two, then WPW_{P} is ultra-log-concave. We do so by formulating an appropriate multivariate analog of WPW_{P} and recognising it as the basis-generating polynomial of a rook matroid.

5.2. Matroidal lifts of PP-Eulerian polynomials

Given a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu, our goal is obtain a suitable poset PP such that the WW-polynomial of PP agrees with the non-nesting rook polynomial of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. We do so in Theorem 5.4. Before we state this, we introduce two multivariate analogs of WPW_{P}: one that is defined only for width two posets and one that can be defined independent of the width; after we show the main theorem for this section we show how one can be obtained from the other.

Given a poset PP on nn elements with a labeling ω\omega, the multivariate (P,ω)(P,\omega)-Eulerian polynomial AP,ω∈ℕ⁡[x1,…,xn,y1,…,yn]A_{P,\omega}\in\mathbb{N}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}] is defined in [BL16] as:

(9) AP,ω​(𝐱,𝐲)=∑σ∈ℒ⁡(P,ω)w⁡(σ),A_{P,\omega}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{L}(P,\omega)}w(\sigma),

where w⁡(σ)w(\sigma) is the following monomial associated to σ\sigma:

w⁡(σ)=∏i∈DB′​(σ)xi​∏j∈AB′​(σ)yj.w(\sigma)=\prod_{i\in\text{DB}^{\prime}(\sigma)}x_{i}\prod_{j\in\text{AB}^{\prime}(\sigma)}y_{j}.

Here the sets DB′​(σ)\text{DB}^{\prime}(\sigma) and AB′​(σ)\text{AB}^{\prime}(\sigma) are defined as follows:

  1. (1)

    DB′​(σ)={σi∈[n]:σi−1>σi}\text{DB}^{\prime}(\sigma)=\{\sigma_{i}\in[n]:\sigma_{i-1}>\sigma_{i}\} is the set of descent bottoms of σ\sigma and σ0≔∞\sigma_{0}\coloneqq\infty.

  2. (2)

    AB′​(σ)={σi∈[n]:σi<σi+1}\text{AB}^{\prime}(\sigma)=\{\sigma_{i}\in[n]:\sigma_{i}<\sigma_{i+1}\} is the set of ascent bottoms and σr+c+1≔∞\sigma_{r+c+1}\coloneqq\infty.

Now we define the multivariate analog of a (P,ω)(P,\omega)-Eulerian polynomial for a width two poset that is similar to AP,ωA_{P,\omega}, but will be more readily recognizable as a basis-generating polynomial of a matroid. Let (P,ω)(P,\omega) be a naturally labelled poset of width two. Then PP consists of a chain C1C_{1} on rr elements and a chain C2C_{2} on cc elements together with cover relations between elements of different chains. Define W~P,ω∈ℕ[xe,ye′:e∈C1,e′∈C2]\widetilde{W}_{P,\omega}\in\mathbb{N}[x_{e},y_{e^{\prime}}:e\in C_{1},e^{\prime}\in C_{2}] as

(10) W~P,ω​(𝐱,𝐲)=∑σ∈ℒ⁡(P,ω)∏i∈DB​(σ)xi​∏j∈CA​(σ)yj,\widetilde{W}_{P,\omega}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{L}(P,\omega)}\prod_{i\in\text{DB}(\sigma)}x_{i}\prod_{j\in\text{CA}(\sigma)}y_{j},

where

  1. (1)

    DB​(σ)={σi∈[r+c]:σi−1>σi}\text{DB}(\sigma)=\{\sigma_{i}\in[r+c]:\sigma_{i-1}>\sigma_{i}\} is the set of descent bottoms of σ\sigma.

  2. (2)

    CA(σ)={σi∈[r+c]:σi<σi+1,σi∈C2}\text{CA}(\sigma)=\{\sigma_{i}\in[r+c]:\sigma_{i}<\sigma_{i+1},\,\sigma_{i}\in C_{2}\} is the set of column ascents, i.e. ascent bottoms of σ\sigma lying in C2C_{2} and σr+c+1≔∞\sigma_{r+c+1}\coloneqq\infty.

The latter condition implies that the element σr+c\sigma_{r+c} is an ascent bottom if and only if σr+c=r+c\sigma_{r+c}=r+c. Here CA\mathrm{CA} stands for column ascent, for a reason that will be made clear during the course of the proof of Theorem 5.4. Also note that W~P,ω\widetilde{W}_{P,\omega} is homogeneous of degree |C2||C_{2}|.

Example 5.3.

Suppose (P,ω)(P,\omega) is the labeled poset in Figure 17. The Jordan–Hölder set is ℒ⁡(P,ω)={24153,21453,12453,21435,24135,12435,21345,12345}\mathcal{L}(P,\omega)=\{24153,21453,12453,21435,24135,12435,21345,12345\}. The polynomial W~P,ω\widetilde{W}_{P,\omega} is a polynomial in the variables x1x_{1}, x3x_{3}, y2y_{2}, y4y_{4}, y5y_{5} and is equal to

W~P,ω=x1​x3​y2+x1​x3​y4+x3​y2​y4+x1​x3​y5+x1​y2​y5+x3​y2​y5+x1​y4​y5+y2​y4​y5.\widetilde{W}_{P,\omega}=x_{1}x_{3}y_{2}+x_{1}x_{3}y_{4}+x_{3}y_{2}y_{4}+x_{1}x_{3}y_{5}+x_{1}y_{2}y_{5}+x_{3}y_{2}y_{5}+x_{1}y_{4}y_{5}+y_{2}y_{4}y_{5}.

Also, recall that if rλ/μr_{\lambda/\mu} is the basis-generating polynomial of the rook matroid on λ/μ\lambda/\mu, then we can express it in terms of row variables x1,…,xrx_{1},\ldots,x_{r} and column variables yr+1,…,yr+cy_{r+1},\ldots,y_{r+c} as

rλ/μ​(𝐱,𝐲)=∑ρ∈NNλ/μ∏i∈R⁡(ρ)xi​∏j∈C⁡(ρ)yjr_{\lambda/\mu}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\sum_{\rho\in\text{NN}_{\lambda/\mu}}\prod_{i\in R(\rho)}x_{i}\prod_{j\in C(\rho)}y_{j}

We can now state the main theorem of the section.

Theorem 5.4.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape and denote by rλ/μr_{\lambda/\mu} and ℓλ/μ\ell_{\lambda/\mu} the basis-generating polynomials of the rook matroid and lattice path matroid on λ/μ\lambda/\mu respectively. There exists a naturally labeled poset (P,ω)(P,\omega) of width two such that

(11) rλ/μ​(𝐱,𝐲)\displaystyle r_{\lambda/\mu}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) ≅W~P,ω​(𝐱,𝐲)\displaystyle\cong\widetilde{W}_{P,\omega}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})
(12) ℓλ/μ​(𝐳)\displaystyle\ell_{\lambda/\mu}(\mathbf{z}) ≅∑σ∈ℒ⁡(P,ω)∏j∈σ⁡(C2)zj\displaystyle\cong\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{L}(P,\omega)}\prod_{j\in\sigma(C_{2})}z_{j}

where ≅\cong denotes equality up to reindexing of the variables.

Remark 5.5.

The fact that linear extensions of posets of width kk bijectively correspond to lattice paths contained within a compact region of ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k} follows from the standard theory of distributive lattices [Sta11, pg. 296]. Similiar bijections to ours also appear in [CPP22, Lemma 8.1] and an unpublished paper of Stanley [Sta] respectively. The theorem above can be seen as a matroidal and multivariate refinement of the aforementioned results.

Proof.

We only address (11), since (12) follows by a similar argument, or alternatively by keeping track of descents and ascents in the bijection provided in [CPP22, Lemma 8.1].

We begin by relabelling the rows and columns of λ/μ\lambda/\mu in the following manner. Denote the innermost lattice path of the skew shape by Lλ/μL_{\lambda/\mu} and number the rows of λ/μ\lambda/\mu from bottom to top and the columns from left to right by the North and East steps of Lλ/μL_{\lambda/\mu} respectively. See Figure 18(a) for an example. Let C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} be the two chains defining PP, labeled respectively by the row and column labels of λ/μ\lambda/\mu that were induced by Lλ/μL_{\lambda/\mu}. Let this labeling be ω\omega. Hereafter, in the context of cover relations, we will use i,ji,j in place of ω⁡(i),ω⁡(j)\omega(i),\omega(j).

Add the cover relation i≺⋅ji\prec\mathrel{\mkern-5.0mu}\mathrel{\cdot}j to PP for every outer corner (i,j)(i,j) of λ/μ\lambda/\mu and similarly the cover relation j≺⋅ij\prec\mathrel{\mkern-5.0mu}\mathrel{\cdot}i for every inner corner (i,j)(i,j). This construction is illustrated in Figure 18(b). The resulting poset is easily seen to be of width two. We make the following claim:

Claim 1: With the labeling as above, for every cell (i,j)(i,j) in the skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu, we have that i<j.i<j.

Proof of claim 1: Since the row labels decrease from top to bottom, it suffices to show this for cell (i,j)(i,j) that is the topmost box in its column. This holds since every topmost box lies directly under the innermost path of the shape.

To see that PP is naturally labeled: consider the cover relation a≺⋅ba\prec\mathrel{\mkern-5.0mu}\mathrel{\cdot}b where a∈C1,b∈C2a\in C_{1},b\in C_{2}. This implies that the (a,b)(a,b) is an outer corner of the shape. Since (a,b)(a,b) is an outer corner, the cell to the left of (a,b)(a,b), say (a,c)(a,c), must lie in λ/μ\lambda/\mu and hence a<ca<c, by the claim above. Since the column labelling increases from left to right, we must also have a<ba<b. The inner corner case is similarly proved.

Now we exhibit a bijection from non-nesting rook placements inside λ/μ\lambda/\mu to elements of the Jordan-Hölder set ℒ⁡(P,ω)\mathcal{L}(P,\omega). This bijection will send non-nesting rook configurations with kk occupied rows to inverses of linear extensions with kk descents. Formally, define f:ℛλ/μ→ℒ⁡(P,ω)f:\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}\to\mathcal{L}(P,\omega) by f=ψ∘Tλ/μf=\psi\circ T_{\lambda/\mu} where Tλ/μ:ℛλ/μ→𝒫λ/μT_{\lambda/\mu}:\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}\to\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} is the rooks-to-outer-corners bijection between rook placements and lattice paths described in the proof of Lemma 3.11 and ψ:𝒫λ/μ→ℒ⁡(P,ω)\psi:\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu}\to\mathcal{L}(P,\omega) is the path-to-permutation map defined by ψ⁡(L)=σ=σ1​…​σr+c\psi(L)=\sigma=\sigma_{1}\ldots\sigma_{r+c}, as in Definition 3.15. An illustration of this is in Figure 19.

Claim 2: The map ff defined above is a bijection.

Proof of Claim 2: By the uniqueness of the permutation representation of the lattice path and the rook-to-path bijection from Proposition 3.11, the map ff is well-defined. To show that ff is a bijection, it suffices to show that ψ\psi is a bijection.

To that end, we first need to show that σ=ψ⁡(L)\sigma=\psi(L) does indeed lie in ℒ⁡(P,ω)\mathcal{L}(P,\omega), whenever LL is a lattice path contained inside λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Suppose i≺⋅ji\prec\mathrel{\mkern-5.0mu}\mathrel{\cdot}j in PP. Two cases arise:

  1. (1)

    Both of i,ji,j lie in the same chain of PP. In this case, they are either both row indices or both column indices; since row indices increase from top to bottom and column indices increase from left to right in the labeling of λ/μ\lambda/\mu, the path LL must traverse step σi−1\sigma^{-1}_{i} before step σj−1\sigma^{-1}_{j} and hence ii must precede jj in σ\sigma.

  2. (2)

    The elements i,ji,j lie in different chains. Assume without loss of generality that ii is a row index and jj is a column index. Then by construction of PP, (i,j)(i,j) must be an outer corner of λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Then the (σi−1)th(\sigma_{i}^{-1})^{\textnormal{th}} and (σj−1)th(\sigma_{j}^{-1})^{\textnormal{th}} steps of LL are respectively 𝚗\mathtt{n} and 𝚎\mathtt{e} steps. Let EE be the lattice path corresponding to the southern boundary of λ/μ\lambda/\mu and let (ψ⁡(E))k=i(\psi(E))_{k}=i, so that (ψ⁡(E))k+1=j(\psi(E))_{k+1}=j. Since (i,j)(i,j) is an outer corner corresponding to a 𝚗𝚎\mathtt{ne} step of LL, the step at which LL takes ii can be no later than kk while the step at which LL takes jj can be no earlier than k+1k+1. This implies that σ\sigma satisfies σi−1≤k<k+1≤σj−1\sigma_{i}^{-1}\leq k<k+1\leq\sigma_{j}^{-1}, as required. The case when i≺⋅ji\prec\mathrel{\mkern-5.0mu}\mathrel{\cdot}j for i,ji,j equal to column and row indices respectively follows by an analogous argument.

This shows that the image of ff lies in ℒ⁡(P,ω).\mathcal{L}(P,\omega).

To see that ψ\psi is a surjection, consider σ∈ℒ⁡(P,ω)\sigma\in\mathcal{L}(P,\omega). Define a lattice path LL by letting the ithi^{\textnormal{th}} step of LL equal σi\sigma_{i}; such a path certainly satisfies g⁡(L)=σg(L)=\sigma but we need to verify that LL is contained inside the shape. Suppose LL exits the skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu. Then there exists an outer corner (i,j)(i,j) of λ/μ\lambda/\mu such that j​iji forms an 𝚎𝚗\mathtt{en} step of LL. In particular σ=σ1​…​j​i​…​σr+c\sigma=\sigma_{1}\ldots ji\ldots\sigma_{r+c}. Now (i,j)(i,j) is an outer corner which implies that i≺⋅ji\prec\mathrel{\mkern-5.0mu}\mathrel{\cdot}j and since σ∈ℒ⁡(P,ω)\sigma\in\mathcal{L}(P,\omega), ii must precede jj in σ\sigma, a contradiction. Thus LL is a valid lattice path in 𝒫λ/μ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda/\mu} and hence gg is a surjection and ff is indeed a bijection.

Claim 3: Let ρ\rho be the rook placement that corresponds to σ\sigma under the bijection ff. Then

f⁡(R⁡(ρ))=DB​(σ)andf⁡(C⁡(ρ))=CA​(σ)f(R(\rho))=\text{DB}(\sigma)\quad\text{and}\quad f(C(\rho))=\text{CA}(\sigma)

That is, ff maps the occupied rows of ρ\rho and the unoccupied columns of ρ\rho to descent bottoms of σ\sigma and ascent bottoms of σ\sigma respectively.

Proof of Claim 3: The map ff acts as follows on occupied row and unoccupied column indices.

f⁡(R⁡(ρ))\displaystyle f(R(\rho)) =ψ⁡({ 𝚗 steps of outer corners of lattice path L=Lρ})\displaystyle=\psi(\{\text{ $\mathtt{n}$ steps of outer corners of lattice path $L=L_{\rho}$}\})
={σiL:σi−1L>σiL}\displaystyle=\{\sigma^{L}_{i}:\sigma^{L}_{i-1}>\sigma^{L}_{i}\}
=DB​(σ),\displaystyle=\text{DB}(\sigma),

and

f⁡(C⁡(ρ))\displaystyle f(C(\rho)) =ψ⁡({ 𝚎 steps of outer corners of lattice path L=Lρ})\displaystyle=\psi(\{\text{ $\mathtt{e}$ steps of outer corners of lattice path $L=L_{\rho}$}\})
={σiL:σiL<σi+1L, σi is a column variable}\displaystyle=\{\sigma^{L}_{i}:\sigma^{L}_{i}<\sigma^{L}_{i+1},\text{ $\sigma_{i}$ is a column variable}\}
={σiL:σiL<σi+1L,σiL∈C2}(since C2 is labeled by column variables)\displaystyle=\{\sigma^{L}_{i}:\sigma^{L}_{i}<\sigma^{L}_{i+1},\sigma^{L}_{i}\in C_{2}\}\quad\text{(since $C_{2}$ is labeled by column variables)}
=CA​(σ).\displaystyle=\text{CA}(\sigma).

This completes the proof of the assertion that W~P,ω\widetilde{W}_{P,\omega} can be written as a multivariate generating polynomial of non-nesting rook placements on λ/μ\lambda/\mu. To finish, we note that after reindexing the row and columns of the skew shape in accordance with the matroid labeling, this latter polynomial is precisely the basis-generating polynomial of ℛλ/μ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda/\mu}. ∎

Remark 5.6.

Note that if skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu has empty rows and columns (for e.g. 5543/52225543/5222) then the resulting poset may have a unique minimal element and/or unique maximal element. In particular the decomposition into chains might not be unique.

Let ℰ\mathcal{E} be the map from Theorem 5.4 that takes a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu to a width two poset PP. From the construction in the proof above, it is implicit that ℰ\mathcal{E} is injective. We record the surjectivity of ℰ\mathcal{E} in the lemma below.

Lemma 5.7.

For every poset PP of width two, there exists a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu such that ℰ⁡(λ/μ)=P\mathcal{E}(\lambda/\mu)=P.

Proof.

While the poset PP has a unique minimum xx, remove xx from PP and designate it as an empty column index. Similarly, while there is a unique maximum yy in PP, remove yy and designate it as an empty row index. Once the poset — which by a minor abuse of notation we continue to denote by PP — has two minimal and two maximal elements, proceed as follows.

Let {t1,…,tr+c}\{t_{1},\ldots,t_{r+c}\} be the elements of PP and let C1,C2C_{1},C_{2} be the two chains of PP of length rr and cc respectively. Define λ/μ\lambda/\mu to be the skew shape with rr rows (labeled from bottom to top by elements of C1C_{1}) and cc columns (labeled from left to right by elements of C2C_{2}) such that:

  1. (1)

    There is an inner corner at (ti,tj)(t_{i},t_{j}) for every cover relation of the form ti≺⋅tjt_{i}\prec\mathrel{\mkern-5.0mu}\mathrel{\cdot}t_{j} where ti∈C2t_{i}\in C_{2} and tj∈C1t_{j}\in C_{1}.

  2. (2)

    There is an outer corner at (ti,tj)(t_{i},t_{j}) for every cover relation of the form ti≺⋅tjt_{i}\prec\mathrel{\mkern-5.0mu}\mathrel{\cdot}t_{j} where ti∈C1t_{i}\in C_{1} and tj∈C2t_{j}\in C_{2}.

By the correspondence between corners and cover relations detailed in the proof of Theorem 5.4, this is precisely the skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu such that ℰ⁡(λ/μ)=P\mathcal{E}(\lambda/\mu)=P. ∎

Remark 5.8.

Let (P,ω′)(P,\omega^{\prime}) be a naturally labeled poset. While Theorem 5.4 and Lemma 5.7 together yield a skew shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu such that (ℰ⁡(λ/μ),ω)(\mathcal{E}(\lambda/\mu),\omega) is a naturally labeled poset satisfying ℰ⁡(λ/μ)=P\mathcal{E}(\lambda/\mu)=P, it might be possible that ω≠ω′\omega\neq\omega^{\prime}. This will not matter for us however, since the polynomial WPW_{P} is independent of the natural labeling.

Theorem 5.4 and Lemma 5.7 together allow one to draw mutually enriching connections between PP-Eulerian polynomials and non-nesting rook polynomials. In one direction, one can use the matroidal properties of Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} to make the strongest possible conclusion for the PP-Eulerian polynomial of width two posets; namely that its coefficient sequence is ultra log-concave. We collect a few other corollaries below, beginning with the precise relation between Brändén and Leander’s multivariate PP-Eulerian polynomial and our modified multivariate width two WW-polynomial. Recall the definition of AP,ωA_{P,\omega} from equation 9.

By Lemma 5.7, every width two poset can be given the natural labeling induced from the skew shape labeling in the proof of Theorem 5.4. We refer to this labeling hereafter as the canonical labeling.

Corollary 5.9.

Let PP be a poset of width two and let ω\omega be the canonical labeling of PP. Then AP,ωA_{P,\omega} is Lorentzian and its support is equal to the collection of bases of a rook matroid.

Proof.

Since the product of Lorentzian polynomials is Lorentzian, AP,ωA_{P,\omega} being Lorentzian would follow from Theorem 5.4 and Lemma 5.7 if we can prove the following identity:

(13) AP,ω​(𝐱,𝐲)=x1​∏i∈C1yi⋅W~P,ω​(𝐱∗,𝐲)A_{P,\omega}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=x_{1}\prod_{i\in C_{1}}y_{i}\cdot\widetilde{W}_{P,\omega}(\mathbf{x}^{*},\mathbf{y})

where 𝐱∗\mathbf{x}^{*} denotes the vector 𝐱\mathbf{x} after the change of variables x1→xmin⁡C2x_{1}\to x_{\min{C_{2}}}. To see why this holds, recall that

AP,ω​(𝐱,𝐲)=∑σ∈ℒ⁡(P,ω)∏i∈DB′​(σ)xi​∏j∈AB′​(σ)yjA_{P,\omega}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{L}(P,\omega)}\prod_{i\in\text{DB}^{\prime}(\sigma)}x_{i}\prod_{j\in\text{AB}^{\prime}(\sigma)}y_{j}

and that 11 must always lie in DB′​(σ)\text{DB}^{\prime}(\sigma). Further, C1⊆AB′​(σ)C_{1}\subseteq\text{AB}^{\prime}(\sigma) for the following reason. For every a∈C1a\in C_{1} and σ∈ℒ⁡(P,ω)\sigma\in\mathcal{L}(P,\omega), let bb be the element succeeding aa in σ\sigma: that is, σ=σ1​…​a​b​…​σn\sigma=\sigma_{1}\ldots ab\ldots\sigma_{n}. If b∈C1b\in C_{1}, we must necessarily have a≺ba\prec b which by the natural labeling ω\omega implies a<ba<b. Similarly, if b∈C2b\in C_{2} and a≺⋅ba\prec\mathrel{\mkern-5.0mu}\mathrel{\cdot}b, it follows that a<ba<b. On the other hand, if b∈C2b\in C_{2} and is incomparable with aa then (a,b)(a,b) must be a cell in the corresponding skew-shape. By claim 11 in the proof of Theorem 5.4, it follows that a<ba<b. Hence a∈AB′​(σ)a\in\text{AB}^{\prime}(\sigma) and C1⊆AB​(σ)C_{1}\subseteq\text{AB}(\sigma). Since every ascent bottom must either be a row or column ascent, we must then have

AB′​(σ)=C1⊔CA​(σ)\text{AB}^{\prime}(\sigma)=C_{1}\sqcup\text{CA}(\sigma)

for every σ∈ℒ⁡(P,ω)\sigma\in\mathcal{L}(P,\omega). Similarly for every σ∈ℒ⁡(P,ω)\sigma\in\mathcal{L}(P,\omega), we have

DB′​(σ)=DB​(σ)⊔{σ1}.\text{DB}^{\prime}(\sigma)=\text{DB}(\sigma)\sqcup\{\sigma_{1}\}.

Note that 1∈DB​(σ)1\in\text{DB}(\sigma) precisely when σ=q​ 1​…\sigma=q\,1\ldots where q=min⁡(C2)q=\min(C_{2}). This implies that qq plays the role of 11 whenever 11 is in DB​(σ)\text{DB}(\sigma), from which (13) follows.

The second statement also follows from (13), Theorem 5.4 and the fact that a coloop is an element that is present in every basis of a matroid. ∎

The next corollary shows that the ultra-log-concavity part of the Neggers–Stanley conjecture is true for naturally labeled width two posets; in particular this holds for Stembridge’s counterexample, shown in Figure 21 and computed in Corollary 5.13. We can deduce an analogous result for the polynomial EP​(t)=∑j=1|P|ej​(P)​tjE_{P}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{|P|}e_{j}(P)t^{j} where ej​(P)e_{j}(P) denotes the number of surjective order–preserving maps from PP to [j][j]. An alternative formulation of the Neggers–Stanley conjecture for naturally labeled posets PP asserts the real-rootedness of EPE_{P}.

Corollary 5.10.

Let PP be a naturally labeled poset of width two and λ/μ\lambda/\mu be the skew shape obtained from Lemma 5.7. Then the WW-polynomial of PP equals the non-nesting rook polynomial of λ/μ\lambda/\mu:

(14) WP​(t)=Mλ/μ​(t),W_{P}(t)=M_{\lambda/\mu}(t),

and hence WPW_{P} is ultra-log-concave. Consequently, EPE_{P} is also ultra-log-concave.

Proof.

Since every natural labeling of the poset PP gives rise to the same WPW_{P}, assume PP has the canonical labeling ω\omega. By Theorem 5.4, the polynomial W~P,ω\widetilde{W}_{P,\omega} is equal, up to a relabeling of the variables, to the basis-generating polynomial of the rook matroid on λ/μ\lambda/\mu. The latter polynomial is Lorentzian, and this property is preserved under a linear change of variables [BH20, Theorem 2.10]. The aforementioned relabeling maps 𝐱\mathbf{x} variables (resp. 𝐲\mathbf{y} variables) labeled by elements of C1C_{1} (resp. C2C_{2}) to 𝐱\mathbf{x} variables labeled by rows 1,…,r1,\ldots,r (resp. columns r+1,…,r+cr+1,\ldots,r+c) of the skew shape. Thus, by specialising the 𝐱\mathbf{x} variables to tt and the 𝐲\mathbf{y} variables to 11 in (11), we obtain (14). The ultra-log-concavity statement of WPW_{P} then follows from Corollary 4.2. Finally, the ultra-log-concavity of EPE_{P} follows from [BFJ24, Lemma 2.5 (ii)]. ∎

Remark 5.11.

By the above corollary and the discussion at the end of Section 4, it follows that for naturally labeled posets PP of width two, Brenti’s conjecture about the log-concavity of WPW_{P} [Bre89, Conjecture 1.1] can be seen as an instance of the Stanley-Yan basis-counting inequality Theorem 4.1.

Another immediate consequence of this correspondence is that Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} has a discrete geometric interpretation — as the h∗h^{*}-polynomial of the order polytope of a naturally labeled width two poset. In [DN23], it was shown that (regular) rook polynomials of a large class of boards are hh-polynomials of the coordinate rings associated to the boards. The poset–skew shape correspondence allows us to deduce a stronger result for non-nesting rook polynomials in the context of skew shaped boards.

Corollary 5.12.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape, PP be the corresponding naturally labeled poset obtained from Theorem 5.4, and 𝒪⁡(P)\mathcal{O}(P) be the order polytope of PP. Then

Mλ/μ​(t)=h𝒪⁡(P)∗​(t).M_{\lambda/\mu}(t)=h^{*}_{\mathcal{O}(P)}(t).

In particular, the h∗h^{*}-polynomial of the order polytope of a naturally labeled width two poset is ultra-log-concave.

Proof.

The proof is immediate from Theorem 5.4 together with the well-known fact that for a naturally labeled poset PP, its PP-Eulerian polynomial coincides with the h∗h^{*}-polynomial of its order polytope; see, for example, [BS18, Theorem 6.3.11]. ∎

In the other direction of the poset–skew shape correspondence, one can use known results on PP-Eulerian polynomials to deduce distributional properties of the non-nesting rook numbers, extending the results in Section 4. We mention two such applications below.

Stembridge’s width two counterexample to the Neggers–Stanley conjecture [Ste07] shows that real-rootedness of Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} can fail in general. This counterexample is illustrated in Figure 21 together with the corresponding skew shape. The following corollary gives a rook theoretic and matroid theoretic context within which Stembridge’s counterexample can be understood.

Corollary 5.13.

The non-nesting rook polynomial Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} is not real-rooted in general. Concretely, Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} is not real-rooted for the skew shape λ/μ=888888765/76654321\lambda/\mu=888888765/76654321.

Proof.

Let λ/μ=888888765/76654321\lambda/\mu=888888765/76654321. Applying the skew shape – poset correspondence Corollary 5.10, we obtain the poset on the left in Figure 21, which we recognize as Stembridge’s counterexample to Neggers’ formulation of the Poset conjecture. Thus Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} is not real-rooted.

Alternatively, using SageMath, we computed Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} to be:

Mλ/μ​(t)=3​t8+86​t7+658​t6+1946​t5+2534​t4+1420​t3+336​t2+32​t+1.M_{\lambda/\mu}(t)=3t^{8}+86t^{7}+658t^{6}+1946t^{5}+2534t^{4}+1420t^{3}+336t^{2}+32t+1.

This polynomial has non-real roots near −1.85884±0.14976​i-1.85884\pm 0.14976i. ∎

Remark 5.14.

By the experimental evidence gathered in [Ste07] and the poset–skew shape correspondence above, it follows that λ/μ=888888765/76654321\lambda/\mu=888888765/76654321 is the smallest skew shape for which Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} fails to be real-rooted. It would be interesting to find a large class of skew shapes for which real-rootedness holds; the conjecture in the next section suggests that Ferrers shapes might be natural candidates for this.

Using the skew shape – poset correspondence, we can also deduce precisely when the non-nesting rook polynomial is palindromic, a fact not immediately obvious from the combinatorics of rook placements alone. The partitions that satisfy this symmetry are defined below.

Definition 5.15.

A partition λ=(λ1,…,λn)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n}) is a squarecase if each of its outer corners lie exactly on the northwest diagonal of the shape.

For an example, see the figure below.
Corollary 5.16.

Let λ/μ\lambda/\mu be a skew shape. Then Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} is palindromic if and only if λ/μ\lambda/\mu is the direct sum of partitions νi\nu_{i} each of which is a squarecase. Moreover, when the shape is a squarecase with nn rows, then

  1. (1)

    Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} is γ\gamma-positive, that is Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} can be written as:

    Mλ/μ​(t)=∑k=0⌊n2⌋γk​tk​(1+t)n−2​k,M_{\lambda/\mu}(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor}\gamma_{k}t^{k}(1+t)^{n-2k},

    where each γi≥0\gamma_{i}\geq 0.

  2. (2)

    In particular, (−1)⌊n2⌋​Mλ/μ​(−1)≥0(-1)^{\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor}M_{\lambda/\mu}(-1)\geq 0.

Proof.

It suffices to show that the result holds for partition shapes with the squarecase property. This is because Mν1⊕ν2=Mν1⋅Mν2M_{\nu_{1}\oplus\nu_{2}}=M_{\nu_{1}}\cdot M_{\nu_{2}} is palindromic if and only each MνiM_{\nu_{i}} is palindromic.

Label the rows of ν=(ν1,…,νn)\nu=(\nu_{1},\ldots,\nu_{n}) with 11 to nn from bottom to top, and the columns n+1n+1 to 2​n2n from left to right. Let QQ be the poset corresponding to ν\nu. By Theorem 5.4, and the reciprocity theorem for PP-partitions, MνM_{\nu} is symmetric if and only if WQW_{Q} is symmetric, which in turn occurs if and only if QQ is graded; that is, all maximal chains of QQ have the same length nn.

This in turn holds if and only if the two chains of QQ are C1={1,…,n}C_{1}=\{1,\ldots,n\} and C2={n+1,…,2​n}C_{2}=\{n+1,\ldots,2n\} and the only non-trivial cover relations are of the form ij≺⋅n+1+iji_{j}\prec\mathrel{\mkern-5.0mu}\mathrel{\cdot}n+1+i_{j} for j=1,…,kj=1,\ldots,k. The latter condition on QQ is equivalent to the outer corners of ν\nu being of the form (ij,n+1+ij)(i_{j},n+1+i_{j}), that is the outer corners lie exactly on the North-West diagonal of ν\nu, which is precisely the definition of a squarecase.

The γ\gamma-positivity of Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} then follows from Theorem 5.4 and [Brä06, Theorem 4.2] while the statement about the sign of Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu} at −1-1 follows from γ\gamma-positivity. ∎

6. Future Work

One of the main results of this paper was the ultra-log-concavity of the polynomial Mλ/μM_{\lambda/\mu}. In the previous section, we noted that real-rootedness holds for special families of λ/μ\lambda/\mu including all skew shapes with rr rows and cc columns with r+c≤16r+c\leq 16. Here we make a conjecture about the real-rootedness of MλM_{\lambda}.

Conjecture 6.1.

Let λ\lambda be a Ferrers shape and let λ−𝟏\lambda-\mathbf{1} denote (λ1−1,…,λn−1)(\lambda_{1}-1,\ldots,\lambda_{n}-1) and let (λ)(i)(\lambda)^{(i)} denote its truncation to its ithi^{\textnormal{th}} part (λ1,…,λi)(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{i}). The non-nesting rook polynomial MλM_{\lambda} is real-rooted. Moreover, the following interlacing relations hold:

Mλ≪Mλ−𝟏andMλ≪∑i=0n−1M(λ)(i).M_{\lambda}\ll M_{\lambda-\mathbf{1}}\quad\text{and}\quad M_{\lambda}\ll\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}M_{(\lambda)^{(i)}}.

See [Brä15] for the definition and applications of interlacing polynomials. Apart from the points mentioned above, we note the following two things in support of the conjecture. One, computational evidence supports this conjecture for all partitions λ\lambda fitting inside a 7×77\times 7 box. Two, a simple interlacing argument shows that for partitions of the form λ=(m,δn)=(m,n,n−1,…,1)\lambda=(m,\delta_{n})=(m,n,n-1,\ldots,1), MλM_{\lambda} is real-rooted.
